items.title: Senate urges INEC to disqualify candidates over violence
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Senate has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to disqualify political candidates found, through established court convictions, to have instigated or participated in electoral violence, irrespective of their party affiliations. The upper chamber also called on state governors to stop denying opposition parties access to public facilities, including hotels and stadia under their control, for political activities. The resolutions followed the adoption of a motion sponsored by Senator Abdul Ningi (Bauchi Central) on Tuesday, expressing concern over the growing incidence of political violence, intolerance and attacks on political leaders and their supporters ahead of the 2027 general elections. The Senate condemned what it described as the increasing frequency and spread of political violence across the country, warning that attacks on political leaders, supporters and political gatherings posed threats to national security, democratic participation and the peaceful conduct of the 2027 elections. It also urged security agencies to conduct impartial and transparent investigations into reported incidents of political violence in Abuja, Edo, Delta and Sokoto states, identify the perpetrators and their sponsors, and ensure their prosecution in accordance with the law. The lawmakers further called on the Federal Government to direct the Inspector-General of Police and other security agencies to strengthen security arrangements for political leaders, candidates, supporters and political gatherings nationwide. They urged the establishment of effective early-warning and rapid-response mechanisms to prevent attacks and other forms of violence ahead of the elections. The Senate also mandated its Committees on National Security and Intelligence, Police Affairs, and INEC to engage relevant institutions and report back within one week on measures to prevent political violence and safeguard the 2027 general elections. The motion followed reported attacks on political figures and gatherings, including the incident involving President Bola Tinubu’s motorcade after he observed Friday prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque, Garki, Abuja. Presenting the motion, Ningi recalled reported attacks on former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi and other political stakeholders in Benue, the disruption of a political procession involving supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress and the Obidient Movement in Asaba, Delta State, on November 7, which reportedly left one person dead and five others injured, as well as an attack on the convoy of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar in Sokoto State. He warned that failure to investigate and prosecute those responsible for political violence could encourage further attacks, deepen political divisions and undermine public confidence in the electoral process. Contributing, Senate President Godswill Akpabio urged INEC to enforce the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026 against electoral violence, stressing that offenders should face the consequences prescribed by law. Akpabio said Sections 121 to 128 of the Act provided for offences relating to electoral violence, intimidation and the snatching of Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) machines, ballot boxes and other electoral materials. He said the lawmakers had recommended penalties ranging from 12 months to five years’ imprisonment, without an option of fine for aggravated offences involving attacks with dangerous objects. According to him, Section 92 also empowers INEC to suspend elections in areas where violence is reported and reschedule them within 24 hours. He added that the Electoral Offences Commission Bill 2025, passed alongside the Electoral Act, provided for a dedicated mechanism to address electoral offences, including vote-buying, violence and attacks on electoral officials. Akpabio said the enactment of the laws placed responsibility on the executive to ensure their effective implementation. In another resolution, following an additional prayer by Senator Sampson Ekong (Akwa Ibom South), the Senate urged the Federal Ministry of Information and the National Orientation Agency to intensify public enlightenment campaigns against political violence. Ekong said legal provisions alone would not adequately address the problem without sustained public awareness, particularly among young people who could be recruited into violent political activities. Also contributing, Senator Binos Yaroe (Adamawa South) urged state governors to ensure that opposition parties and candidates were not denied access to public facilities, including arenas and hotels controlled by state governments. He said restrictions on such facilities could undermine the principle of a level playing field for political parties and create avoidable political tensions. Senator Ali Ndume (Borno South) supported the motion and proposed that security agencies prohibit the carrying of dangerous weapons during political campaigns. He called for the arrest of anyone found carrying knives, sticks or other harmful objects at campaign venues, irrespective of political affiliation. Ndume also proposed the establishment of mobile courts to ensure the prompt prosecution of offenders during campaign activities. He said political campaigns should be conducted with legitimate campaign materials rather than weapons, adding that the measures should apply equally to all political parties, including the ruling All Progressives Congress. Ndume further cautioned against campaign slogans that could heighten political tensions, citing slogans such as “Tinubu Must Go”, “Atiku Must Go” and “Obi Must Go”. He said political disagreements should be resolved through peaceful engagement rather than violence. Senator Sumaila Kawu (Kano South) also expressed concern over the presence of supporters carrying dangerous weapons at political gatherings. Kawu described it as a shame for candidates contesting elections into the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship positions to be surrounded by supporters carrying weapons. He questioned the conduct of politicians who, despite making laws against electoral violence, allowed their supporters to engage in activities capable of undermining the electoral process. “It is a shame to see candidates contesting for the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship surrounded by supporters carrying dangerous weapons. Where are we going as lawmakers when we appear to encourage conduct that violates the laws we enacted?” he said. The Senate urged political parties, candidates and their supporters to embrace peaceful political engagement and respect the rule of law ahead of the 2027 general elections. The post Senate urges INEC to disqualify candidates over violence appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: COP31: African workers declare ‘no more empty promises’ as unions demand climate justice, decent jobs
items.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young Representing 18 million organised workers across 52 African countries, the International Trade Union Confederation–Africa, ITUC-Africa, has challenged world leaders at COP31 to move beyond climate change rhetoric and deliver concrete action, demanding climate finance, decent green jobs, workers’ protection and a just transition that puts African workers at the centre of decision-making. The African workers, under the banner of ITUC-Africa, issued the message at the COP31 Political March in Antalya, Turkey, declaring that the continent’s workforce would no longer tolerate empty promises and delayed commitments on climate action. In a statement by its General Secretary, Akhator Joel Odigie, the regional labour organisation warned that African workers were bearing the devastating consequences of climate change despite contributing comparatively little to the crisis. Speaking under the theme, “Deliver, Don’t Delay – Move from Dialogue to Action,” Odigie said the climate emergency was no longer an abstract environmental concern but an immediate threat to workers’ lives, livelihoods and fundamental labour rights. “We are the 18 million organised workers of Africa, represented here by ITUC-Africa across 52 countries. We are the ones who build, transport, farm, mine, and power this continent. And we are the ones who will pay the highest price if COP31 ends in more talk and no delivery,” he declared. He stressed that workers were already experiencing the devastating effects of extreme weather conditions, including unbearable workplace heat, destructive flooding and prolonged droughts that threaten agricultural production and community livelihoods. “The climate crisis is not abstract for us. It is the unbearable heat on a construction site, the flood that destroys a community, the drought that kills a harvest,” Odigie stated. Citing International Trade Union Confederation data, he disclosed that extreme workplace heat already claims nearly 19,000 lives annually, while heat stress could wipe out working hours equivalent to 136 million full-time jobs by 2030. “This is a labour rights crisis. And it demands a labour response,” he insisted. Workers reject slow progress on climate commitments ITUC-Africa expressed concern that despite COP31 being presented as the “COP of implementation,” progress on translating climate commitments into tangible benefits for workers and vulnerable communities remained inadequate. The organisation particularly criticised the slow progress on the Just Transition Work Programme, arguing that workers’ rights and participation must not be relegated to the margins of climate negotiations. According to Odigie, although procedural progress had been recorded, the mechanism’s design remained unresolved, with no substantive agreement reached on how it would operate. “The Just Transition Work Program—the one space where workers’ rights should be front and centre—has made procedural progress, but its mechanism design is still open, with no substantive agreement yet,” he said. He maintained that the ongoing negotiations in Antalya represented a critical opportunity to move from discussions to concrete commitments that would guarantee workers a meaningful role in shaping the continent’s economic and environmental future. Demands climate finance, not debt A major concern raised by the African labour movement is the persistent inequality in global climate financing, particularly the limited resources reaching African countries despite the continent’s vulnerability to climate change. ITUC-Africa noted that while the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap seeks to mobilise $1.3 trillion annually by 2035, sub-Saharan Africa receives less than three per cent of global climate finance, with much of the funding provided through loans rather than grants. The organisation also highlighted the funding gap surrounding the Loss and Damage Fund, stating that although $826 million had been pledged, only $456 million had actually been received. Odigie further expressed disappointment that the African Group of Negotiators’ push to triple adaptation finance had not received a standalone agenda slot. He argued that African countries should not be forced to accumulate more debt to address a climate crisis they contributed relatively little to creating. “So when we say ‘deliver,’ we mean: stop congratulating yourselves on roadmaps and start signing the cheques, with grants, not debt,” he declared. The labour movement called on developed countries to provide new, additional, predictable and adequate climate financing, primarily through grants and highly concessional public financing. It also demanded debt relief, progressive taxation and windfall taxes on extractive industry profits as alternative ways of mobilising resources for climate action and essential public services. “Africa should not be forced to borrow its way out of a crisis it did not cause. We reject loans as climate contributions,” the statement stressed. New form of economic colonialism ITUC-Africa also warned that the global transition to clean energy must not become another avenue for exploiting Africa’s natural resources while denying its people the economic benefits of industrialisation. The organisation argued that Africa must move beyond exporting unprocessed critical minerals, including lithium and cobalt, and develop the capacity to process these resources locally. It insisted that the continent’s mineral wealth should support industrial development, create decent employment opportunities and improve the living standards of African workers. “The global energy transition must not become a new colonialism. Africa must use this shift to industrialise, not remain a supplier of unprocessed raw materials,” Odigie declared. He called for local processing of critical minerals to ensure that the jobs and economic opportunities generated by the global green transition remain within African economies. The organisation also warned against the potential impact of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on African producers and workers, arguing that the costs of the global transition should not be unfairly transferred to developing economies. Another major demand is the establishment of an effective Just Transition Mechanism that guarantees workers formal representation and meaningful influence over decisions concerning employment, investment and industrial transformation. ITUC-Africa maintained that workers must be involved in designing and implementing national transition pathways rather than being subjected to decisions reached without their participation. It called for the operationalisation of a mechanism capable of providing technical assistance, capacity-building and financial support to countries pursuing climate-friendly economic transformations. “A mechanism without worker participation is a shell. Trade unions must have formal representation and meaningful influence—not token consultations—in decisions affecting employment, investment, and industrial transformation,” he said. He added that the proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be developed in partnership with workers and their representative organisations. “The proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be built with us, not for us,” he emphasised. Protect jobs, workers’ safety The African trade union body further demanded comprehensive employment and social protection measures to ensure that the transition to a green economy does not leave millions of workers unemployed or economically vulnerable. It called for employment-impact assessments, skills development, retraining, redeployment opportunities, job or income guarantees, occupational safety and health protections, and universal social protection to be incorporated into every transition plan. The organisation stressed that women, young people, migrant workers and those employed in the informal economy required specific protection because of their vulnerability to economic and environmental disruptions. Particular attention was drawn to extreme workplace heat, which ITUC-Africa said must be formally recognised as an occupational hazard, with enforceable safety measures introduced to protect workers. The organisation argued that climate policies would remain incomplete if they addressed environmental sustainability without guaranteeing decent working conditions, employment security and social protection. In a message, ITUC-Africa warned that COP31 must not become another international climate conference where vulnerable populations are asked to wait while governments and global institutions continue making promises without delivering results. Odigie argued that the consequences of global warming were already being felt, making urgent action essential to prevent African workers from bearing an even greater share of the crisis. “The question is not whether we will transition—the question is whether that transition will be just, or whether it will leave millions of African workers behind while a few extract the profits of a green economy built on our backs,” he warned. He insisted that African workers were not attending the climate negotiations merely to appeal for sympathy but to demand their rightful place in decisions that would determine their economic future. “We are not here to beg. We are here to negotiate. We are here to demand. And we are here to stay,” he declared. Reaffirming the organisation’s position, he outlined four central demands: climate finance through grants rather than debt; an operational Just Transition Mechanism with workers fully represented; African industrialisation rather than continued extraction of raw materials; and decent, green and unionised jobs for the continent’s workforce. He said: “Deliver the finance—grants, not debt. Deliver the Just Transition Mechanism—with workers inside, not outside. Deliver industrialisation—not extraction. Deliver decent, green, unionised jobs for Africa’s workers.” Odigie concluded with a call for world leaders to translate their climate commitments into measurable outcomes, stressing that African workers would continue to press for accountability and justice. “Move from dialogue to action, now,” he declared, ending his address with the rallying cry, “Amandla!” The post COP31: African workers declare ‘no more empty promises’ as unions demand climate justice, decent jobs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Lutte contre l’émigration irrégulière : 50 personnes interpellées à Yoff et Toubab Dialaw
items.description: La gendarmerie nationale a mené deux opérations contre l’émigration irrégulière dans les localités de Yoff Ndenatte et de Toubab Dialaw, les 16 et 17 novembre 2026. Ces interventions, conduites par les unités de Dakar et de Rufisque, ont permis l’interpellation de 50 personnes, dont quatre présumés passeurs. À Yoff Ndenatte, la brigade territoriale de Foire a procédé, le 16 novembre, à l’arrestation de 16 individus. Parmi eux figurent un présumé passeur et 15 candidats à l’émigration, dont trois femmes. Le lendemain, une seconde opération menée par la brigade territoriale de Yenne, à Toubab Dialaw, a abouti à l’interpellation de 34 personnes, dont trois présumés passeurs et 31 candidats au départ. Au cours de ces interventions, les gendarmes ont également mis la main sur un important lot de matériel destiné à la traversée maritime. La saisie comprend notamment des moteurs de pirogue, des appareils GPS, une boussole, des badges ainsi que des provisions alimentaires. Les investigations se poursuivent afin de déterminer les responsabilités des personnes interpellées et d'identifier d'éventuels réseaux impliqués dans l'organisation de ces départs clandestins. C.G.D

items.title: De Rubens al siglo XX: tres siglos de pintura revelan cómo el retrato de la silueta femenina fue perdiendo sus curvas
items.description: Desde la Venus de Willendorf, la figurilla del Paleolítico de grandes senos y aún más grandes caderas , a la Helena Fourment saliendo del baño que pintó Pedro Pablo Rubens a mediados del siglo XVII, la representación de la mujer ha tendido a destacar sus curvas, relacionándolas con su capacidad reproductiva. Pero desde hace tres siglos, la silueta de las mujeres retratadas se ha ido haciendo menos sinuosa: se ha reducido progresivamente la diferencia entre cintura y cadera ( índice cintura-cadera, ICC ). Eso es lo que muestra, al menos, un trabajo en el que han seguido la evolución de la forma femenina en centenares de retratos pintados desde el Barroco y hasta mediados del siglo XX. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Afghanistan: Children on the Move: Displacement Leaves Afghan Children Hungrier and More Vulnerable, Save the Children Warns
items.description: Country: Afghanistan Source: Save the Children KABUL, 18 November 2026 – More than half of children displaced in Afghanistan said they have less food to eat since leaving their homes, while two in five reported worsening health, according to a new Save the Children report that reveals the severe toll displacement is taking on children across the country. The “Children on the Move” report, based on interviews with more than 800 children and caregivers in seven provinces in Afghanistan, found that displacement over the past three years has deepened hunger, disrupted education and exposed children to heightened protection risks. More than nine in 10 children surveyed had experienced displacement or migration. More than half (55%) of children said they had less food to eat after moving, 41% said their health had deteriorated, and a third (33%) of caregivers said children's access to education had worsened. But despite growing needs, support is failing to reach many children. Fewer than one in 10 children surveyed said they had received any assistance, while nine in 10 said they needed support to access food. The findings come after more than 6.67 million Afghans have returned from Pakistan and Iran since September 2023 – increasing the population by up to 14% - and putting greater pressure on families and communities already struggling with poverty, food insecurity and repeated crises. [2]. Afghanistan also has one of the highest rates of internal displacement globally, with about 7 million people , or around 14% of the population, displaced as of 2025. [3]. Economic hardship is the main driver of displacement in Afghanistan. Nearly half of children (49%) said their families moved because they could not find work or earn enough income, while a third cited food shortages. Almost one in four said their families had relocated due to deportation or pressure to leave another country. Nearly seven out of 10 children surveyed have endured two or more crises in the last three years, including drought, floods, earthquakes and conflict. Compounding crises and displacement are affecting children’s wellbeing in Afghanistan, with children facing growing protection risks. Just over one in 10 (11%) said they had been exposed to at least one protection risk, including child labour, physical or verbal violence or early marriage. Caregivers reported that girls faced particularly high risks during displacement journeys and after arriving in new locations. Among those affected is Nooria*, 8, who arrived in Afghanistan for this first time earlier this year after her family left Pakistan where they had built their lives over five decades. Nooria*, her parents and three siblings arrived with little more than the clothes they carried. Nooria* said: “We returned from Pakistan. We had a home there, and I had many friends. I like Afghanistan too, but I miss my school and my friends. We used to play together and laugh a lot. “We want to have a school like the one we had in Pakistan, where we can continue our education.” Nooria’s family cannot afford the transport costs to send her to school, but she attends classes at a Save the Children temporary learning space. Her mother, Nazoo*, 28, said: “My husband does not have a job here, and we have no source of income to provide for our children's needs. I worry every day about how we will find food for our next meal. “When you are born in a country and get married there, that place becomes your home. You feel that you belong there. When you suddenly have to leave, your whole life falls apart, especially when you arrive with nothing.” The ‘Children on the Move’ report found that assistance reaching children is extremely limited, with significant gaps between needs and the support they receive. Ashish Damle, Country Director, Save the Children in Afghanistan said: “No child should have to abandon their homes, schools and communities for safety or survival - but for many, displacement has become part of their childhood. Children face dangerous journeys with serious protection risks, only to arrive in places where their families are still struggling to put food on the table, access healthcare and send them to school. “Our ‘Children on the Move’ research reveals a deeply concerning reality - finding a new home does not mean reaching safety. Girls and children with disabilities in particular face greater protection risks, while poverty is forcing families to make impossible choices just to survive, often with little or no humanitarian assistance. “Children who have already lost their homes should not be left to face these risks alone. We urgently need sustained funding to protect them along migration routes and ensure they can access essential services wherever they settle. “These children deserve more than day to day survival. They deserve the chance to feel safe, return to school and rebuild their lives.” Save the Children has been working in Afghanistan since 1976, including through periods of conflict, displacement and natural disasters. We currently run programmes in nine provinces and work with partners across an additional 11 provinces, delivering services in health, nutrition, education, child protection, shelter, water, sanitation, hygiene and livelihoods. References: Multimedia content: https://www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4M1TH4VWH9 * Denotes name changed to protect identity [1] Key findings: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/children-on-the-move-research-study-afghanistan-2026 . Save the Children’s ‘Children on the Move’ study in Afghanistan was conducted in selected locations affected by floods, droughts, earthquakes, and conflict, identified as migration source, transit, and destination areas. The primary study population was children on the move aged 0–17 years and their families. 824 children and 838 caregivers were interviewed through structured questionnaires and 32 qualitative consultations conducted with key informants and caregiver groups in July 2026. The study covered seven provinces; Nangarhar, Herat, Balkh, Faryab, Kabul, Kandahar and Sar-e-Pul. The findings are representative of Save the Children operational areas covered by the study, not of Afghanistan as a whole. [2] Number of returnees as of 31 October 2026 from UN and partners. Population increase calculation using UN population figure of 48.6m https://www.unocha.org/afghanistan [3] https://www.internal-displacement.org/database/displacement-data/ For interview requests and further information, please contact: Rachel Thompson, Media Manager, Asia: Rachel.thompson@savethechildren.org Our media out of hours contact is media@savethechildren.org.uk / +44(0)7831 650409

items.title: Polémique sur « Marrakech pour les riches » : le ministre du Tourisme précise ses propos
items.description: Après la polémique suscitée par ses précédentes déclarations sur les prix et l’offre touristique à Marrakech, le ministre du Tourisme, de l’Artisanat et de l’Économie sociale et solidaire, Jalal Charf, a tenu à clarifier sa position mardi devant la Chambre des conseillers. Il assure que Marrakech reste « une ville pour tous les Marocains » et nie avoir voulu réserver la destination aux touristes aisés. La polémique autour des propos de Jalal Charf sur le tourisme à Marrakech est revenue au-devant de la scène, mardi, lors de la séance des questions orales à la Chambre des conseillers. Face aux interrogations suscitées par ses précédentes déclarations sur l’offre touristique et le niveau des prix dans la ville ocre, le ministre a voulu mettre les choses au clair. Il a notamment rejeté toute interprétation selon laquelle Marrakech serait appelée à devenir une destination réservée aux catégories les plus aisées. « Marrakech est une ville pour tous les Marocains » , a-t-il affirmé, assurant qu’il ne revenait ni au gouvernement ni à lui-même de déterminer qui peut visiter la ville. « Je ne suis pas celui qui décide qui visite Marrakech » Le ministre a expliqué que ses précédents propos s’inscrivaient dans une réflexion sur l’équilibre entre l’offre et la demande touristiques, et non dans une volonté de catégoriser les visiteurs selon leurs revenus. Selon lui, chaque visiteur doit pouvoir trouver à Marrakech une offre correspondant à ses moyens financiers, quel que soit son niveau de revenu. Le véritable problème résiderait plutôt dans l’insuffisance de l’offre touristique abordable, notamment pour les visiteurs à la recherche de prestations adaptées aux budgets modestes ou intermédiaires. Dans cette logique, Jalal Charf a mis en avant le rôle de l’État dans la stimulation de l’investissement et l’élargissement de l’offre afin de mieux répondre à la demande et, à terme, de contribuer à une maîtrise des prix. Vers davantage de diversité dans l’offre touristique Le ministre a également défendu une approche fondée sur la justice sociale et territoriale. La justice territoriale doit, selon lui, permettre d’étendre le développement touristique à l’ensemble des régions du Royaume, tandis que la justice sociale suppose la mise en place d’une offre suffisamment diversifiée pour répondre aux capacités financières des Marocains comme des visiteurs étrangers. Cette mise au point intervient alors que la question du coût des séjours à Marrakech alimente régulièrement le débat sur l’accessibilité du tourisme intérieur. La ville reste l’une des principales destinations touristiques du Royaume, mais la hausse des prix de l’hébergement et de certaines prestations pose la question de la capacité du secteur à répondre aux attentes des différentes catégories de visiteurs. Le gouvernement prépare une réforme du guidage touristique Au-delà de la polémique autour de Marrakech, le ministre a annoncé une autre réforme concernant la profession de guide touristique. Le Maroc compte actuellement 4 657 guides touristiques agréés. Jalal Charf considère cette profession comme un élément essentiel de l’offre touristique nationale, les guides étant notamment chargés de transmettre aux visiteurs l’histoire, la culture et le patrimoine du Royaume. Le gouvernement envisage ainsi une révision globale du cadre juridique régissant la profession, notamment pour traiter la question des guides non agréés et favoriser l’intégration des professionnels exerçant en dehors du secteur organisé. Le ministre souhaite engager cette réforme en concertation avec les professionnels afin de préserver les droits acquis des guides agréés tout en ouvrant davantage l’accès à la profession. De nouvelles conditions d’accès à la profession ? Parmi les pistes évoquées figure la possibilité de mieux prendre en compte l’expérience professionnelle acquise, mais aussi de faciliter l’accès au métier à certains profils universitaires, notamment les doctorants et titulaires d’un doctorat en histoire ou dans d’autres disciplines pertinentes. Le ministre estime également que le potentiel de développement du métier reste important dans les zones rurales et montagneuses. Il juge notamment problématique que certains sites touristiques disposant d’un patrimoine naturel ou culturel important puissent accueillir des visiteurs sans qu’il soit toujours facile d’y trouver un guide agréé. Le gouvernement prévoit de travailler, au cours des trois prochains mois, sur les grandes lignes de cette réforme. Mettre fin aux régularisations exceptionnelles Concernant les guides non agréés, Jalal Charf a rappelé que la profession est encadrée par la loi 12.05 et que deux opérations exceptionnelles de régularisation ont déjà été menées, en 2018 et en 2023. Pour le ministre, multiplier ces régularisations ne permettrait toutefois pas de résoudre durablement le problème. De nouveaux professionnels pourraient en effet apparaître et réclamer à leur tour une mesure similaire. Le gouvernement privilégie donc une réforme du cadre légal, notamment des conditions d’accès actuellement liées au niveau d’études, à la formation, à l’âge ou encore à l’obligation de se déplacer vers certains centres, notamment Tanger et Ouarzazate. L’objectif affiché est de parvenir à un équilibre entre l’ouverture de la profession à de nouvelles compétences, la protection des guides agréés et la lutte contre l’informel, tout en accompagnant la croissance du secteur touristique marocain. The post Polémique sur « Marrakech pour les riches » : le ministre du Tourisme précise ses propos appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Ouahbi : "Notre premier objectif est atteint"
items.description: Au terme de la victoire du Maroc face au Niger (1-0), synonyme de qualification pour la phase finale de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations CAN-2027, le sélectionneur national, Mohamed Ouahbi, s’est félicité d’atteindre le premier objectif, tout en affichant ses ambitions pour la suite des qualifications. « Le premier objectif est atteint, celui de la qualification. Nous allons désormais travailler avec sérieux pour atteindre d’autres objectifs, notamment la première place » , a déclaré Ouahbi en conférence de presse d’après-match. Le technicien marocain a relevé plusieurs points positifs dans la prestation de ses joueurs, tout en pointant un manque d’intensité en seconde période. « En première mi-temps, nous étions meilleurs. En deuxième période, nous avons manqué d’intensité, surtout dans les courses », a-t-il reconnu. Le sélectionneur a également insisté sur la nécessité de prendre le temps d’analyser cette rencontre et d’échanger avec les joueurs afin de maintenir le même niveau d’engagement et de poursuivre le travail de progression. Malgré les absences enregistrées, Ouahbi s’est montré satisfait de la contribution des nouveaux jeunes joueurs, estimant qu’ils méritaient pleinement leur place au sein de la sélection. « Nous avons joué avec le même sérieux, mais nous voulons toujours progresser pour arriver à la CAN dans les meilleures conditions et essayer de la gagner » , a souligné le sélectionneur, qui s’est également montré confiant quant au potentiel technique et physique de son groupe. « Nous avons de très bons joueurs, techniquement et physiquement. Nous serons de plus en plus en forme » , a-t-il conclu. Pour sa part, le sélectionneur du Niger, Nabil Neghiz, est revenu sur les efforts fournis par son équipe pour corriger les insuffisances constatées lors de la première confrontation entre les deux sélections, qui s'était soldée par une lourde défaite nigérienne (5-1). « Nous avons essayé de corriger certaines choses par rapport au premier match, lors duquel nous avions été lourdement battus » , a expliqué Neghiz. Il a également mis en avant les qualités de la sélection marocaine, notamment sur le plan technique et sa capacité à trouver des solutions dans le jeu. Malgré cette nouvelle défaite, le sélectionneur du Niger garde espoir pour la suite de la campagne qualificative. « Il nous reste deux matches et nous sommes optimistes pour le reste des qualifications », a-t-il assuré. The post Ouahbi : "Notre premier objectif est atteint" appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 120 marmites par jour et une solidarité sans faille : Dans les coulisses de l’accueil des rapatriés à Bobo-Dioulasso
items.description: En visite d'inspection le lundi 16 novembre 2026 au stade Sangoulé Lamizana de Bobo-Dioulasso, le ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le Lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kaboré, a salué le fonctionnement efficace de la chaîne d'accueil déployée en faveur des compatriotes contraints de quitter la Guinée. Entre prise en charge médicale, enregistrement et préparation quotidienne de plus de cent marmites de nourriture, la solidarité nationale a permis d'offrir un abri digne aux arrivants alors que l'opération de rapatriement touche désormais à sa fin. Au stade Sangoulé Lamizana, l'émotion du retour se conjugue avec la rigueur d'une organisation logistique rodée. Le lundi 16 novembre 2026, le ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le Lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kaboré, a parcouru l'ensemble des installations aménagées pour recevoir les compatriotes contraints d'abandonner la Guinée. Du système d'enregistrement aux espaces d'hébergement, en passant par le stock de vivres, l'infirmerie et la grande cuisine, chaque maillon de la chaîne a fait l'objet d'un examen attentif afin d'évaluer les conditions de travail des équipes mobilisées et la qualité de la prise en charge des familles. Au cœur du site, l'effort culinaire illustre à lui seul l'ampleur de la réponse humanitaire. Chaque jour, les équipes préparent entre 110 et 120 marmites (numéro 30) afin d'assurer la restauration de la foule accueillie au stade. Marquant sa proximité avec les acteurs de terrain, le ministre s'est prêtée à un geste symbolique en remuant elle-même la marmite aux côtés des femmes mobilisées, rendant hommage à leur dévouement exemplaire. Malgré la forte pression liée à l'afflux massif de personnes refoulées, l'évaluation générale demeure très satisfaisante, témoignant d'une prise en charge humaine et structurée qui préserve la dignité de chacun. L'opération de rapatriement amorce désormais sa phase finale. Lors de la séance de débriefing organisée avec les responsables du site, il a été confirmé que le flux de retour tire vers sa fin. Seuls quelques derniers autocars traversant actuellement le territoire malien restent attendus pour ramener les ultimes contingents vers la mère Patrie. Alors que de nombreux compatriotes accueillis à Bobo-Dioulasso ont déjà pu regagner leurs localités d'origine, le Lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kaboré a exhorté l'ensemble des équipes à maintenir un niveau de vigilance et d'engagement maximal jusqu'à l'arrivée du tout dernier convoi. L’article 120 marmites par jour et une solidarité sans faille : Dans les coulisses de l'accueil des rapatriés à Bobo-Dioulasso est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Grève à Orabank : la médiation de la BCRG dans l’impasse, syndicat et direction campent sur leurs positions
items.description: Alors que les guichets d’Orabank Guinée sont restés fermés ce mardi 17 novembre, en raison du mot d’ordre de grève générale et illimitée lancé par la section syndicale de l’établissement, la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) a tenté une médiation entre les différentes parties. Elle a ainsi reçu successivement les représentants des travailleurs, ceux de la direction générale de la banque ainsi que des responsables de la Fédération syndicale autonome des banques, assurances et microfinances de Guinée (FESABAG). À l’issue de ces échanges, la Banque centrale a clairement invité la direction générale à trouver une issue à la crise dans la journée, afin de permettre une reprise effective des activités dès ce mercredi. Dans cette perspective, le régulateur a demandé aux protagonistes de se retrouver directement au siège d’Orabank pour tenter de parvenir à un compromis. Un nouveau rendez-vous leur a été fixé à 14h30, dans les locaux de la BCRG, en vue de la signature éventuelle d’un protocole d’accord. Mais cette tentative de conciliation a rapidement tourné court. À la grande surprise des représentants du personnel, la direction générale a maintenu sa position, affirmant ne pas être en mesure de satisfaire les revendications syndicales dans l’immédiat. Elle a indiqué devoir, au préalable, consulter son conseil d’administration, au plus tard vendredi prochain. Une perspective de report que la délégation syndicale a jugée inacceptable, rejetant catégoriquement le calendrier proposé par la direction. Malgré l’attente prolongée jusqu’en soirée, dans l’espoir de voir émerger une nouvelle proposition susceptible de débloquer la situation, aucune autre offre n’a été formulée par la direction générale. Faute d’avancée concrète, le mouvement de grève se poursuit donc chez Orabank Guinée. Une situation qui fait planer l’incertitude sur la reprise des activités et l’accès aux services bancaires pour des milliers de clients à travers le pays.

items.title: NDIC urges corps members to save in insured banks
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu AWKA — The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) has urged members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in Anambra State to cultivate sound financial habits and ensure they save their money in banks insured by the corporation. The advice was given during a financial literacy and sensitisation seminar organised by NDIC officials at the NYSC orientation camp in Awka South Local Government Area of the state. The corporation urged the corps members to embrace what it described as a smart financial lifestyle built around earning, saving, investing and spending wisely. The Communications Manager of NDIC, Chinenye Chimezie-Amadi, advised the corps members to exercise caution when choosing where to save their money, stressing the importance of using deposit-taking institutions insured by the corporation. She urged them to develop the habit of budgeting, distinguishing between their needs and wants, and setting aside part of their earnings for emergencies and future investments. According to her, many people earn money without keeping track of how they spend it, making it difficult for them to build savings. “Our presence at the orientation camp is to help you learn a kind of life you need to live in future as you begin to make decisions for yourselves. “Some people won’t have savings, but you see them carrying expensive hairs and mobile phones. That is living a false life. We are looking at a situation where you save for emergency and for your future,” she said. Amadi urged the corps members not to dismiss the possibility of saving because of their present earnings, saying even small amounts could accumulate into substantial savings when set aside consistently. She also advised them to prioritise essential expenses before discretionary spending and develop the habit of paying themselves first by setting aside a portion of their income. On the choice of financial institutions, she warned against depositing money in unregulated schemes offering unusually high returns, urging them to verify that their banks were insured by NDIC. “Even when you have a house, you still need to set aside your house rent as a way of saving. If you do it consistently, you will be surprised at the amount you save,” she said. The NDIC Controller, Enugu Zonal Office, Mr Chidi Nwankwo, urged the corps members to acquire financial literacy skills ahead of their transition from national service into the labour market. Speaking on the topic, ‘Know Your Deposit Protection: A Practical Guide for NYSC Corps Members’, Nwankwo explained the corporation’s role in protecting depositors and outlined the applicable deposit insurance limits. He advised the corps members to confirm that any deposit-taking bank with which they intended to transact was insured by NDIC, explaining that eligible deposits were protected within the limits prescribed for different categories of financial institutions. According to him, deposits in deposit money banks are insured up to N5 million per depositor, while those in microfinance banks, primary mortgage banks and payment service banks are covered up to N2 million. Using an example, Nwankwo explained that a depositor with N6 million in a deposit money bank that subsequently fails would receive insurance compensation of up to N5 million, while recovery of the remaining N1 million would depend on the realisation of the failed bank’s assets. He encouraged the corps members to understand the scope of deposit insurance and make informed financial decisions to protect their savings. The post NDIC urges corps members to save in insured banks appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: EU advances Syrian recovery and reconstruction through Syria Partnership Coordination Forum in Damascus
items.description: Country: Syrian Arab Republic Source: European Commission Please refer to the attached file. Today, the Syria Partnership Coordination Forum (SPCF) convened in Damascus for the first time to advance Syria's recovery and reconstruction, showcase investment opportunities and agree on concrete steps forward. The SPCF brought together key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab countries, and the UN and International Financial Institutions, such as the World Bank, the European Investment Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the Islamic Development Bank, as well as civil society, to discuss Syria's business environment and steps to translate Syria's priorities into concrete investment opportunities. The Forum, co-chaired by Syria and the EU, was opened by Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica and the Syrian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Assaad Al-Shaibani. Economic revitalisation, institutional recovery and improved livelihoods In her second visit to the country, Commissioner Šuica officially launched the Syria Technical Assistance Hub to support Syrian institutions in strengthening their capacities and advancing reforms that are instrumental to restore confidence, attract responsible investment and support sustainable economic recovery. The Commissioner also witnessed the signing of new EU-funded contracts supporting Syria's recovery and reconstruction, namely on the rule of law, on an enabling business environment andon support to small and medium-sized enterprises . These initiatives will help revive the economy, strengthen public institutions and improve livelihoods. By helping businesses access finance and grow, the projects can create jobs and improve conditions for investment. They will also improve access to justice, supporting a recovery that benefits people across Syria. During her bilateral meeting with Minister Al-Shaibani, Commissioner Šuica received Syria's signed undertaking to implement the EU's Registered Exporter system . This marks an important step towards enabling Syrian products to benefit from preferential access to the EU market under the Generalised Scheme of Preferences, opening up new opportunities for Syrian exporters and supporting the country's economic recovery. Commissioner Šuica also visited the Deir Ali Power Plant together with Ibrahim Al-Adhan, Syrian Deputy Minister of Energy and EIB Vice President Gelsomina Vigliotti. The visit highlighted the importance of restoring Syria's energy infrastructure for economic recovery and explored opportunities for future EU engagement in the energy sector with other international partners. Background After the fall of the Assad regime at the end of December 2024 and following the Brussels IX Conference of 17 March 2025, Syria and the EU launched the SPCF, which provides a platform to align partners' support on Syria's recovery priorities and coordinate on their implementation. The Forum is instrumental in facilitating structured engagement among key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab nations, and International Financial Institutions. The SPCF is structured under regular senior-official plenary meetings at capital level, and regular practical level. It builds on the EU's support for Syria's recovery. During her first visit to Damascus in June 2025, Commissioner Šuica announced €175 million to help Syria rebuild its institutions, advance transitional justice and revive its economy. In January 2026, President Ursula von der Leyen announced around €620 million in EU support for 2026–2027 to support recovery and provide humanitarian aid. In May 2026, the Council restored the full application of the EU–Syria Cooperation Agreement, paving the way for stronger trade ties. On 16 November 2026, EU Foreign Ministers supported moving ahead with the EU-Syria Association Agreement. In December, a Day of Dialogue will take place for the second time in Damascus, organised by the Syrian authorities, Syrian civil society and the EU. It will provide a platform for inclusive dialogue on Syria's transition and the role of civil society. For more information EU support to Syria - factsheet The EU announces €175 million to support recovery in Syria EU opens new chapter in its relations with Syria Quote(s) A peaceful, stable and inclusive Syria is important for Syrians, to the region and to Europe. The EU is ready to deepen its partnership with Syria as Syrians rebuild their country for all citizens. At today’s Forum in Damascus, we focused on what international partners and businesses can do to support the country’s own priorities, so people can find jobs, businesses can reopen and services can further be restored. Gestion foncière : le gouvernement durcit le ton contre les attributions illégales de terrains de l’État
items.description: Le Ministère de l'Urbanisme, de l'Habitat et de l'Aménagement du Territoire monte au créneau. Dans un communiqué officiel publié au Journal télévisé de la RTG ce mardi 17 novembre, les autorités dénoncent la persistance d'occupations et de cessions illégales de terrains étatiques, orchestrées par des acteurs non habilités. Dans ce document, le Ministère de l'Urbanisme et de l'Habitat rappelle que la gestion et l'attribution des domaines fonciers de l'État obéissent à un cadre légal strict. Aussi, il insiste sur un point fondamental : l'unique autorité habilitée à instruire et attribuer les terrains relevant du domaine public est le ministère compétent. Par conséquent, les maires, chefs de quartier, responsables communautaires et autres intermédiaires n'ont en aucun cas le droit de se substituer à l'administration centrale pour octroyer des cessions, attributions ou autorisations d'occupation. Sanctions et poursuites judiciaires à l'horizon La mise en garde est claire : tout acte délivré en violation de ces dispositions réglementaires sera immédiatement annulé ou retiré. Les contrevenants, qu'il s'agisse d'autorités locales complices ou de simples citoyens, s'exposent à de lourdes sanctions administratives ainsi qu'à des poursuites judiciaires. Le ministère appelle ainsi l'ensemble des populations à la plus grande vigilance. Pour tout projet d'acquisition de terrain ou demande d'autorisation, les usagers sont tenus de se tourner exclusivement vers les services officiels du ministère de l'Habitat afin de garantir la régularité de leurs démarches. Le domaine de l'État étant inaliénable par des voies informelles, le gouvernement appelle à la responsabilité collective pour faire respecter la loi.

items.title: Ghana’s nuclear journey: From Nkrumah’s vision to a new investment commitment
items.description: Ghana’s proposed US$200 million investment in nuclear power readiness marks a significant step in a journey that began more than six decades ago. It renews an ambition rooted in the country’s earliest development agenda: building the energy capacity to sustain industrialisation and economic transformation. During a recent discussion in the media, I expressed support for this investment. Its importance becomes clearer when placed within the history of Ghana’s efforts to include nuclear power in its electricity generation mix. In 1961, under President Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana decided to undertake the Ghana Nuclear Reactor Project. Its immediate purpose was to establish a research reactor for scientific research, training and radioisotope production. The longer objective was to develop the human resources and technical knowledge necessary for nuclear electricity generation. The establishment of the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission gave that ambition an institutional foundation. Nuclear science formed part of a broader vision in which education, infrastructure and energy would support an industrial economy. Nkrumah recognised that economic transformation required deliberate preparation for future electricity demand. Factories, mineral processing facilities and expanding cities would need dependable power. His overthrow in 1966 interrupted the early nuclear power agenda, although Ghana’s scientific work in nuclear technology continued. An important milestone followed during President Jerry John Rawlings’ administration. The Ghana Research Reactor, GHARR-1, achieved first criticality in December 1994 and was formally commissioned in March 1995. It served research and training purposes, giving Ghanaian scientists practical experience in reactor operations and nuclear applications. That experience helped strengthen the country’s technical foundation for future development. The modern policy drive towards nuclear electricity gained renewed momentum during the energy difficulties of the 2000s. In 2007, President John Agyekum Kufuor’s administration established a presidential committee chaired by Professor Daniel Adzei Bekoe to assess the potential role of nuclear power. Its recommendations informed Cabinet’s decision in 2008 to include nuclear energy in Ghana’s electricity generation mix. Successive administrations continued the preparatory work. A major legal development came during President John Dramani Mahama’s first administration with the passage of the Nuclear Regulatory Authority Act, 2015, Act 895. The Act established an independent regulatory authority and provided a framework for licensing, inspection, enforcement and the protection of people and the environment from radiation risks. This legal foundation is central to the credibility of Ghana’s ambitions. Nuclear power requires institutions capable of examining technical proposals, enforcing standards and holding operators accountable throughout the life of a facility. Regulatory competence must develop alongside the programme itself. Ghana’s preparations also underwent international scrutiny. The International Atomic Energy Agency conducted an Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2017 and a follow-up mission in 2019. In 2022, under President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, Ghana formally announced its transition into Phase Two of the programme, involving preparatory work towards construction following a policy decision. This history reflects contributions by successive governments, scientists, engineers and public institutions. It demonstrates the value of continuity in national development. Projects requiring decades of preparation depend on administrations preserving institutional knowledge and advancing the work they inherit. The latest commitment under President Mahama’s administration provides an opportunity to move that work forward with a defined funding proposal and timetable. The 2027 Budget proposes US$200 million for a 24-month nuclear readiness programme, running from January 2027 to December 2028. The preparations include site studies, technology selection, environmental assessment, financing, licensing, safeguards, emergency planning and the safety case. The stated target is to complete readiness and sign an engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract for a fully state-owned nuclear power plant by December 2028. The nature of this commitment must be communicated accurately. The US$200 million is intended for readiness activities. It represents preparatory expenditure rather than the full construction cost of a nuclear plant. The Budget also explicitly recognises that completing readiness in 2028 does not mean nuclear electricity generation will begin in that year. That distinction should help establish realistic public expectations. The quality of preparation will influence the project’s eventual cost, safety, financing and delivery. My support for this investment rests on the need to plan for Ghana’s future productive capacity. Our electricity policy must account for the demands of an economy seeking to manufacture more goods, process more of its natural resources and support increasingly sophisticated businesses. Nuclear power deserves consideration within that long-term planning. Its suitability must be assessed alongside other generation sources, the capacity of the national grid, financing conditions and projected demand. The objective should be a dependable electricity system that supports competitive production. There is also an opportunity to build Ghanaian skills and expand participation in a technically demanding industry. A nuclear programme can create work across engineering, construction, environmental management, law, finance, security and technical services. The extent to which Ghanaians benefit will depend on deliberate training, credible local participation requirements and opportunities for domestic businesses. Training must therefore be connected to identifiable roles. Universities, technical institutions and professional bodies should be involved early enough to prepare people for the work the programme will require. Local participation must similarly be supported by standards, certification and supplier development. As a lawyer and energy policy analyst, I consider governance fundamental to the success of this investment. Transparent procurement, rigorous technology assessment and financing terms that protect the public interest must guide implementation. The regulator must have the resources, expertise and independence to make decisions on safety grounds. Communities must receive clear information and meaningful opportunities to participate. Waste management, emergency preparedness and eventual decommissioning must be incorporated into planning and financing from the outset. These requirements give substance to the investment. Public confidence will grow through demonstrable competence, openness and accountability. Ghana’s nuclear journey has endured interruptions, renewed commitments and years of institutional preparation. The proposed investment offers President Mahama’s administration an opportunity to advance this national undertaking through measurable progress. The task now is to turn funding commitments into sound decisions, capable institutions and a credible route towards implementation. That is how an ambition first pursued in the early years of independence can contribute to Ghana’s next stage of development. Our energy ambition must match our development ambition. The writer is a lawyer, law lecturer, author and energy and public policy analyst.

items.title: Médias d’État : le président Doumbouya offre cinq Fortuner aux cinq animatrices des émissions Kibaro de la RTG
items.description: Dans une ambiance marquée par l'émotion et la reconnaissance, la Radiodiffusion Télévision Guinéenne (RTG) a abrité une cérémonie de remise de véhicules à cinq femmes journalistes émérites. Un geste fort des autorités visant à saluer leur dévouement au service public de l'information. La cérémonie s’est déroulée au sein de l'enceinte de la RTG, en présence du ministre de la Communication, de l'Économie numérique et de l'Innovation, Fana Soumah, de la Directrice générale de l'institution, ainsi que de nombreux responsables et agents. Hawa Keïta, Julienne Lamah, Bountouraby Sylla,, Mariama Saranké Camara et Rabiatou Diallo ont chacune reçu les clés d'un véhicule tout-terrain flambant neuf. Ce don, apporté ce mardi par le ministre Secrétaire général de la présidence de la République, le Général Amara Camara, et le ministre Directeur de Cabinet de la Présidence, Djiba Diakité, témoigne de la haute attention que le chef de l'État, le général Mamadi Doumbouya, porte aux professionnels des médias. Pour les bénéficiaires, ce geste dépasse le simple cadre matériel. Il vient prolonger la reconnaissance officielle déjà actée à travers leur élévation au rang de Chevalier de l'Ordre national du mérite, intervenue en octobre 2026. Prenant la parole, le ministre Fana Soumah a exprimé sa profonde satisfaction face à cette marque de considération présidentielle envers ces femmes battantes de la télévision nationale. Il a tenu à souligner l'impact de leur travail au quotidien et l'importance de pérenniser de telles actions pour encourager l'excellence et l'abnégation dans le secteur des médias publics.

items.title: Child Online Africa calls for AU action on online violence against children
items.description: Child Online Africa has called on the African Union (AU) and its member states to take urgent and coordinated action to protect children from online violence, sexual exploitation and other forms of digital abuse. The organisation has launched the #AfricaESafetyNow campaign ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, scheduled for November 18 to 19, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. In a statement issued on Tuesday, November 17, the organisation said Africa had reached a critical point in addressing the risks children face as they increasingly engage with digital platforms. It acknowledged that technology provides opportunities for learning, innovation and development but warned that children are also exposed to online violence, cyberbullying, harmful content and sexual exploitation. “The protection of children online can no longer be treated as an optional policy concern or left entirely to individual families. It is a shared responsibility that requires decisive leadership, coordinated continental action and accountability from governments and technology companies,” the statement said. Child Online Africa wants the AU to move beyond policy commitments and establish concrete measures to protect children across digital spaces. Its proposals include the development of a continental legal framework or protocol on child online safety, with clear and enforceable protection standards. It is also calling for a dedicated African eSafety Commission, or an equivalent continental mechanism, to coordinate action and ensure accountability among member states. The organisation further wants the AU to accelerate implementation of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy through a clear and adequately funded roadmap. Other recommendations include expanding age-appropriate digital literacy and online safety education in schools and communities, while strengthening the capacity of parents, teachers and caregivers. It also urged governments to hold technology companies accountable through safety-by-design measures, stronger privacy safeguards, effective reporting systems and appropriate enforcement. The organisation acknowledged the AU’s adoption of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy in 2024 as an important recognition of the need to protect children online. However, it said the policy must now be backed by political commitment, institutional coordination and adequate investment. “What is now required is the political will, institutional coordination, investment and accountability to translate that commitment into meaningful protection for children,” the statement said. Ahead of the Manila conference, Child Online Africa said African countries should approach the discussions with a common position on protecting children from violence in both physical and digital environments. It argued that online safety should form an integral part of the broader child protection agenda, rather than being treated as a separate concern. “Violence against children does not end at the school gate or stop when a child enters the digital world. Online safety must be recognised as an integral part of the broader child protection agenda,” the statement said. The organisation is calling on African governments, civil society groups, child-rights advocates, parents, educators, young people, development partners and technology companies to support the campaign. It is urging the public to sign its petition, share its message and demand concrete action from the AU. The petition, titled Africa’s Children Are Under Attack Online: Demand the African Union Act Now to Save Them! , seeks to turn public concern into pressure for measurable policy action. “Africa’s children deserve more than promises. They deserve protection,” the statement said. The statement was signed by Awo Aidam Amenyah, Executive Director of Child Online Africa, an Accra-based organisation advocating for child online protection across the continent. items.title: Jensen Huang and the Myth of Indispensability
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Jensen Huang said in a statement this morning that he would be “honored” to return to Nvidia, the computer-chip giant from which he was ousted just last week. Unfortunately for Huang, the company’s board made it clear on today’s earnings call that it’s not considering rehiring him. But major figures in Silicon Valley have been making a show of their continued support. For another, less powerful executive, reports of extramarital affairs with three women —one of whom is alleged to be a Chinese spy and another of whom was a direct subordinate—would likely be seen as irredeemable lapses in judgment. Yet Huang’s endorsers don’t seem to view this as the end of his career at the company. “Without Jensen,” Elon Musk claimed on X this weekend, Nvidia will lose important “handshake” deals that Huang personally negotiated. Gavin Baker, whose firm invests in Nvidia, has written that he’s in favor of reinstating Huang as the investigations play out. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney remarked on X that “journalists with sketchy motives” effectively “gaslit” the board into pushing out a “once-in-generation visionary.” An Uber co-founder, Travis Kalanick, who knows a thing or two about tech ousters , was among the more than 195,000 signatories of a petition to reinstate Huang as the company’s CEO—as were Musk, Baker, and Sweeney. The Wall Street Journal reports that a high-level Nvidia employee sent a letter to the company’s board warning that “irreplaceable talent” might leave if Huang isn’t reinstated. When President Trump was asked yesterday whether he’d support the return of Huang, a close ally, he told reporters, “I would not mind that.” Ultimately, none of these people has full control over Huang’s fate. That power belongs to Nvidia’s board of directors. But the support for Huang, despite his clearly disqualifying transgressions, is a testament to the power that this one man has held over Nvidia and the economy at large. (It may also be informed by the dramatic firing and rehiring of another tech titan: Sam Altman.) Even though Huang is accused of having jeopardized national security, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is now reportedly probing whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws, his backers insist that he remains indispensable. Their argument is that he is the company, and that the risks of losing him might actually outweigh the risks of bringing him back as CEO. In a way, they are right: Huang has made himself synonymous with Nvidia. But his centrality is a liability rather than an asset. This moment should be a reckoning about the risks of relying so heavily on any one CEO—yet many in the industry are reinforcing the opposite lesson, doubling down on a disgraced executive. Nvidia is what you might call a “systematically important” institution—industry lingo for a company whose failure would destabilize parts of the financial system. Wall Street trembled after the revelations about Huang spurred a roughly $1.5 trillion sell-off in Nvidia stock (equivalent to more than 25 percent of the company’s value). The AI sector, and in turn the entire U.S. economy, is heavily dependent on the firm’s chips. “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation,” my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote last week. “Huang is too big to fail. Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now.” Some of this is owed to the myth of the tech leader as an irreplaceable genius—a story that Silicon Valley loves to tell. As The Washington Post points out , nearly a tenth of the value of the S&P 500 is tied to companies with no clear successor: Nvidia, Tesla, and Meta. Huang himself liked to boast about his famously flat org structure—he had 60 direct reports. The New York Times notes that Nvidia’s board, which is now investigating whether Huang was the target of Chinese espionage, has a history of “loyalty and deference” to him. Some of its directors have been on the board since 1993. Public outcry has been an effective tactic in bringing back ousted tech leaders in the past; in late 2023, OpenAI’s board fired Altman because he “was not consistently candid in his communications” with them—but reinstated him five days later after a company-wide revolt. Like Huang, Altman is a celebrity co-founder. He’s the face of his company and the person seen as largely responsible for its success. Any of Altman’s shortcomings or misdeeds were considered secondary to, and distinct from, his ability to generate value for shareholders. Obviously, this isn’t the first case of an executive facing consequences over a relationship with an employee: McDonald’s fired its CEO over this in 2019, Intel’s CEO resigned in 2018 after failing to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, Boeing pushed out its CEO in 2006 over a similar situation. The ongoing national-security concerns add another layer of urgency to the situation. The question of how much Huang actually knew about Megaspeed—the company that the alleged Chinese spy worked for, which the U.S. Department of Commerce has been looking into since 2024—is currently under investigation. Investors are angry enough that they’re suing Nvidia over the fiasco (the company had initially denied that there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about its CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive until Huang himself admitted to it; Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment). Not everyone is pushing for Huang’s comeback. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has suggested that he’d like to see Nvidia pick a new CEO from outside the company, and some lawmakers have opposed the idea of Huang’s return. But those who want him reinstated are selling a dangerous narrative about the indispensability of any one leader. The celebrity investor Balaji Srinivasan wrote today that “it’s arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company”—never mind that Nvidia, under Huang, may have been responsible for allowing the United States’ biggest economic rival to access top-tier computer chips. Tying an entire enterprise to the success or failure of a single person comes with extreme risks; Huang’s defenders are ignoring them. Related: A scandal at the center of the economy The spectacular rise and fall of Jensen Huang Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : David Frum: Why does Rubio sound so nasty lately? The Iran war has slipped into a dangerous limbo. Do Republican states have a better quality of life? Maxwell Taylor Kennedy: Trump’s arch must be stopped. Today’s News The United States has lost its measles-elimination status for the first time since 2000 , after more than a year of continuous transmission amid declining vaccination rates, the Pan American Health Organization announced. More than 7,700 cases and 10 deaths have been reported since last January, raising concerns that large outbreaks could become more common. The National Security Agency’s highly classified internal-communications network went down today, prompting staggered employee arrivals as officials investigated the disruption, CNN reported. White House officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and the agency noted that backup systems would allow it to continue sharing urgent intelligence with President Trump and allied countries. Anthropic is considering raising the price of its initial public offering to more than $80 a share amid strong investor demand, potentially valuing it at up to $1.6 trillion. The AI company is expected to finalize its share price tomorrow ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut, on Thursday. An Almost Entirely Unregulated Corner of the Health-Care Workforce By Olga Khazan When Mariah Stockman went into labor with her first child, her husband called their doula and told her to come to the hospital right away. Despite the urgency of the situation, the doula, Stockman said, asked her husband if she had time to stop and get a coffee. Two and a half hours later, the doula walked into Stockman’s delivery room. “I’ll never forget the coffee in her fucking hand,” Stockman told me recently. Her doula, she said, caught only the last 10 or so minutes of her labor, and she didn’t visit after the baby’s birth, as they had agreed on. Stockman said she paid $2,500 for the doula’s services: “What a waste.” Read the full article. items.title: CAN 2027: le Burkina bat la Mauritanie (3-1) et se qualifie
items.description: Les Etalons du Burkina Faso se sont qualifiés pour la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations (CAN) 2027 en battant (3-1) les Mourabitounes, ce mardi 17 novembre 2026, au stade Olympique de Nouakchott en Mauritanie. L'équipe nationale du Burkina Faso a obtenu son ticket de qualification pour la 36e édition de la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations (CAN). Les poulains du sélectionneur Amir Abdou ont battu la Mauritanie par trois buts à un à Nouakchott, dans le cadre des matchs éliminatoires, ce mardi 17 novembre 2026. Les Etalons ont vite pris le dessus sur leurs adversaires mauritaniens en marquant leur premier but à la 11e minute de jeu grâce à à Aboubacar Sidiki Camara avant que l'attaquant Franck Lassina Traoré ne marque le deuxième but à la 28e minute. A la 75e minute, les Mourabitounes parviendront à réduire le score sur un but de Ali Dadié, redonnant espoir à leurs supporters. Mais les Burkinabè vont mettre fin à l'espoir des Mourabitounes en marquant le troisième but à la 89e minute grâce au jeune recrue de la sélection nationale, Moïse Elohim Kaboré. Dans ce Groupe F composé aussi du Bénin et de la Centrafrique, ce sont les Béninois et les Burkinabè qui ont obtenu leur qualification pour la CAN 2027 qui sera co-organisée par le Kenya, l'Ouganda et la Tanzanie du 19 juin au 18 juillet 2027. Par Bernard BOUGOUM L’article CAN 2027: le Burkina bat la Mauritanie (3-1) et se qualifie est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
