items.title: Ogun 2027: PDP, APC clash over Adebutu’s chances
items.description: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Ogun State have exchanged words over the 2027 governorship election, following the PDP’s prediction that its candidate, Ladi Adebutu, would win between 18 and 19 of the state’s 20 local government areas. While the PDP expressed confidence in Adebutu’s electoral prospects, the ruling APC dismissed the projection as political fantasy, insisting that the opposition party lacked the structures and grassroots support to secure victory. The spokesperson for the 2027 PDP Governorship Campaign Council in Ogun State, Wale Adedayo, made the prediction during an interview on Arise Television, monitored on Sunday. Adedayo, a journalist and former Chairman of Ijebu East Local Government, said Adebutu would defeat the APC candidate, Senator Solomon Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, despite the influence of federal power and the ruling party’s political structures. He predicted that the PDP would win all six local government areas in Ogun Central, the entire Ogun East Senatorial District and at least two local government areas in Ogun West. “PDP will clear between 18 to 19 local government areas in Ogun. I can assure you of that. Adebutu will win Ogun East, Adebutu will win the six LGAs of Ogun Central and a minimum of two in Ogun West,” he declared. He argued that the political support demonstrated by some APC members and attendees at the ruling party’s events would not necessarily translate into votes, expressing confidence that many would eventually support the PDP candidate. “It is not the noise that makes things happen. When it comes to the real show, those who are following them know the party they will vote for,” he said. Adedayo attributed the PDP’s anticipated victory partly to what he described as widespread dissatisfaction with the country’s economic situation, claiming that voters would reject the hardship associated with the present administration. On the possibility of the APC deploying federal influence to retain power in the state, he cited the 2023 governorship election in Ogun and the recent electoral experience in Osun State as examples of how such influence could be resisted. “The federal might was there in 2023, it didn’t work. Federal might was there in Osun State and it didn’t work, and it won’t work again this time,” he said. Adebutu’s candidature Adedayo also commended the judiciary over its intervention in the dispute surrounding Adebutu’s candidature, following a court decision that restored his name to the list of candidates submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). He faulted INEC’s initial removal of Adebutu’s name, arguing that the commission ought to have sought clarification from the PDP, which submitted the party’s membership register. According to him, the responsibility for determining party membership rests with the political party rather than the electoral commission. “The PDP submitted the register and not INEC. It is the party that can prove who is a member and who is not a member. It is not INEC. The judgment of the court was very sound. INEC ought to have written to the party that submitted the list rather than removing his name from the list,” he said. He further maintained that INEC had monitored the PDP governorship primary and recognised Adebutu as its winner, alleging that the controversy surrounding his candidature was politically motivated. Adedayo claimed that the development was intended to weaken the opposition party and discourage its members ahead of the election. He, however, said the controversy had not disrupted the party’s campaign activities, adding that Adebutu and his running mate, Hajia Lateefat Sowunmi-Kolapo, had continued visiting communities across the state to canvass support and present their manifesto. “Those who orchestrated the thing wanted to demoralise members, but Ladi Adebutu continued with his campaign, and that is how he has been going round all villages and towns in Ogun State, meeting with the people. “It didn’t stop our programme; we have been moving around. Seeing the leaders coming out to campaign boosted the morale of PDP members and supporters. There won’t be any battle in Ogun State,” he said. On the PDP’s proposed development agenda, Adedayo identified grassroots development and local government autonomy as key priorities of an Adebutu-led administration. He said the PDP candidate had promised to strengthen local government administration, revive moribund farm settlements, improve food production and provide functional healthcare facilities and potable water in rural communities. “Ogun State is on a true path for real development because all our health centres must work. The farm settlement must be revived by all means, and their output in terms of food production must increase. There will be potable water in all villages,” he said. He added that local government autonomy would enable elected council officials to deliver essential services and address challenges facing rural communities. Adedayo also questioned Adeola’s ancestry, alleging that the APC candidate had not adequately clarified issues surrounding his identity and origin. APC fires back However, the APC dismissed the PDP’s projection, describing it as unrealistic and evidence of the opposition party’s alleged disconnect from grassroots political realities. In a statement, the APC State Publicity Secretary, Comrade Femi Nuberu, challenged Adedayo to concentrate on rebuilding the PDP rather than making what he described as exaggerated electoral predictions. Nuberu argued that the PDP had been weakened by internal crises, leadership disagreements, defections and the departure of prominent political figures, insisting that the party lacked the organisational capacity to deliver the projected victory. He cited the defection of former Ogun PDP Chairman, Hon. Sikirullahi Ogundele; former State Publicity Secretary, Akinloye Bankole; and former State Youth Leader, Oyejide Sunkanmi, among other party chieftains, as evidence of the opposition party’s alleged declining fortunes. He also recalled the defection of six PDP members of the Ogun State House of Assembly in March 2026 and the departure of former PDP Deputy Governorship Candidate, Hon. Adekunle Akinlade. According to him, the loss of elected representatives, influential leaders and grassroots mobilisers had raised questions about the PDP’s ability to compete effectively across the state. Nuberu described the PDP as an “empty political shell”, accusing Adedayo of creating false expectations about the opposition party’s electoral strength. “How can a party that has lost touch with political reality suddenly boast of winning 18 out of 20 local government areas? Is Wale Adedayo merely making these claims to create false hope and mislead a desperate governorship aspirant? “The PDP is an empty shell, and its spokesperson should stop mistaking political propaganda for genuine electoral strength,” he said. The APC spokesman also questioned the PDP’s organisational capacity, asking where its structures, leaders and grassroots mobilisers were. He further accused Adedayo of making the projections for personal political survival, arguing that the PDP’s previous record in government had eroded public confidence in the party. Nuberu also raised issues surrounding the 2023 governorship election, alleging that the PDP candidate had faced court proceedings over allegations of vote-buying and electoral offences. He cautioned the opposition party against presenting procedural court orders as final judicial pronouncements on outstanding political and electoral disputes, insisting that ongoing legal matters should be understood within their proper context. Responding to Adedayo’s dismissal of federal influence, Nuberu maintained that Ogun remained firmly under APC control, declaring that the ruling party had no intention of surrendering its political structures and grassroots strongholds. He attributed the APC’s confidence to its established political network, grassroots mobilisation and what he described as the achievements of the state government in infrastructure, education, healthcare, economic opportunities and security. According to him, residents were more interested in sustaining the state’s development trajectory than in what he called the political theatrics of opposition politicians. The APC spokesman went further to predict that the PDP would struggle to win even a single ward out of the state’s 236 wards. “From our assessment of the political atmosphere across the state, the PDP will struggle to win even a single ward out of the 236 wards in Ogun State. The 2027 election will expose the true strength of every political party,” he said. Nuberu urged APC members and supporters to remain united and intensify efforts to strengthen the party’s structures ahead of the 2027 general elections, reaffirming its determination to retain power in the state. items.title: Dinar algérien : le dollar poursuit sa montée sur les deux marchés
items.description: Le dollar US poursuit sa tendance haussière face au dinar algérien tant au taux officiel et sur le marché de change parallèle. L’euro reste en revanche stable au marché noir et recule au taux de la Banque d'Algérie. Le billet vert américain a enregistré plusieurs records historiques face à la monnaie algérienne ces dix derniers jours au marché de change officiel. Le dollar fonce vers le seuil de 140 dinars au taux de change officiel De 136,13 dinars lundi 9 novembre, le dollar a clôturé la semaine dernière à 136,68 dinars, vendredi 13 novembre. Il a entamé la nouvelle semaine lundi toujours à la hausse à 136,71 DA pour s'établir ce mardi 17 novembre à 136,84 dinars pour un dollar. La monnaie américaine n'est plus qu'à quelques centimes de 137 dinars et fonce sur le seuil psychologique de 140 dinars pour un dollar. Un dollar pour 250 dinars au marché noir n'est plus loin Sur le marché parallèle, le dollar se dirige aussi vers un seuil psychologique, celui de 250 dinars pour un dollar qui n'est plus très loin. Ce mardi au square Port-Saïd, principale place de change parallèle d'Alger, le dollar est échangé pour 247,5 dinars, soit 24 750 dinars pour 100 dollars. Lundi 9 novembre, le billet vert s’échangeait pour 245,5 dinars. La hausse est de deux dinars en dix jours. L’euro pourrait bientôt passer sous la barre des 150 dinars sur le marché officiel L’euro ne connaît pas la même courbe. Au taux officiel, il a enregistré plusieurs baisses successives face au dinar, passant de 152,90 DZD le 9 novembre à 151,66 DA jeudi dernier pour d'établir ce mardi à 150,78 dinars. Un euro sous la barre des 150 dinars est désormais très envisageable à court terme, très loin du record absolu de 162,77 dinars pour un euro enregistré en janvier 2021. La monnaie européenne stable face au dinar au marché parallèle Sur le marché noir, la monnaie unique européenne est stable. Ce mardi 17 novembre, elle est cotée à 276 dinars pour un euro, soit le même taux enregistré lundi 9 novembre. Le resserrement de la valeur face au dinar algérien de l'euro et du dollar suit la tendance sur les marchés internationaux où la monnaie européenne et le billet vert américain se dirigent vers la parité. Le taux a fluctué ce mardi entre 1,09 et 1,1 dollar pour un euro. Le dollar est à son plus haut niveau depuis mai 2025, porté principalement par les anticipations sur les taux d’intérêt de la Réserve fédérale américaine (FED). L’article Dinar algérien : le dollar poursuit sa montée sur les deux marchés est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Two die, Gombe APC chairman, campaign DG injured in crash
items.description: By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe The Gombe State Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Mohammed Dantata Ndus, and the Director-General of the party’s 2027 Governorship Campaign Council, Sa’du Hassan, have sustained injuries in a road accident that claimed two lives in Dasan Yunusa community. The accident occurred on Tuesday along the Deba-Talasse Junction while the two party officials were travelling to join the campaign entourage of Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya in Balanga North Local Government Area of the state. The APC State Campaign Council confirmed the incident in a statement, identifying the deceased as Haruna and Kabiru, both indigenes of Dasan Yunusa. It said the two APC chieftains sustained injuries and were receiving medical attention at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Gombe. Preliminary accounts indicated that the accident occurred when the driver conveying the party officials reportedly swerved to avoid a head-on collision with a motorcycle carrying three persons, which allegedly appeared suddenly at the junction. The vehicle reportedly veered off the road in the process, resulting in the fatal incident. Confirming the accident, the Gombe State Sector Commander of the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Samson Kaura, said he had received information about the incident but was awaiting comprehensive details. Kaura confirmed that the APC chairman and the campaign council’s Director-General were receiving treatment, adding that further information would be provided as investigations progressed. The campaign council expressed sorrow over the incident and extended its condolences to the bereaved families, the people of Dasan Yunusa and others affected by the tragedy. Meanwhile, Governor Yahaya, who was leading the APC campaign activities in the area, visited Dasan Yunusa following news of the accident to commiserate with the bereaved families and community leaders. The governor described the incident as painful and unfortunate, noting that the loss of two lives had cast a shadow over what was intended to be a day of political engagement with the people. He urged the bereaved families and residents to accept the tragedy as the will of Almighty Allah. Yahaya prayed for the repose of the souls of the deceased in Aljannatul Firdaus and for strength for their families to bear the loss. As part of efforts to support those affected, the governor donated N5 million to the families of the deceased and the community leadership. He also prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured, particularly Ndus and Hassan, who were reported to be stable and responding to medical care. The governor’s visit and donation followed the fatal accident that disrupted the party’s campaign activities in the area. The post Two die, Gombe APC chairman, campaign DG injured in crash appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Burkina Faso : La Fondation Coris offre 360 tricycles aux VDP agricoles
items.description: Le Bureau national des grands projets du Burkina (BN-GPB) a reçu, ce 17 novembre 2026, un important lot de matériel roulant de la part de la Fondation Coris. Il est destiné aux 8 000 Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) agricoles formés dans le cadre de l’Initiative présidentielle pour la production agricole et l’autosuffisance alimentaire (IP-P3A). Ce sont, au total, 360 tricycles qui ont été offerts aux 8 000 VDP agricoles de la première cohorte de l’IP-P3A. Ce don vise à aider ces jeunes agriculteurs, réunis en coopératives, à s'installer progressivement pour débuter leurs activités. Selon Inoussa Ouédraogo, coordonnateur de l’IP-P3A, cette action matérialise une vision du président du Faso rendue possible grâce à l'accompagnement de la Fondation Coris. Celle-ci consiste à soutenir les jeunes du monde rural afin qu'ils s'approprient pleinement le secteur de l'agriculture. « La dotation en moyens roulants, tels que les tricycles, fait partie des grandes préoccupations de ces jeunes pour leur déplacement et surtout pour l'évacuation de leur production. Les résultats sont palpables sur le terrain et ces jeunes, aujourd'hui, n'attendent que ça, vraiment pour apporter un plus à la production et à l'atteinte de l'autosuffisance alimentaire qui est vraiment une source de notre intégrité », a indiqué Inoussa Ouédraogo. La remise officielle des tricycles©️Faso7 Ces moyens roulants ont coûté 500 millions de FCFA à la Fondation Coris. Selon Emmanuel Sawadogo, président de la fondation, ce don s'inscrit dans le cadre de la responsabilité sociale de Coris Bank. Au-delà de cet aspect, c'est une réponse à l'appel du président du Faso pour accompagner les initiatives de développement en cours. « Fidèles à sa mission d'intérêt général, nous avons voulu nous ranger aux côtés des autorités pour répondre financièrement à cet appel pour doter les VDP de 360 motos. Nous espérons que les VDP pourront faire œuvre utile et bon usage de ces motos », a-t-il indiqué. Les VDP agricoles ont exprimé leur joie de recevoir ce don. Ils ont fait savoir que ce matériel va leur être utile pour leurs déplacements et faciliter l'acheminement des récoltes vers les magasins de stockage. Ils se sont engagés à être des modèles pour accomplir les objectifs assignés. « Être VDP agricole, c'est déjà un grand engagement. À notre tour, ce que nous pouvons faire, c'est de les rendre fiers et de mener à bien la mission qu'on nous a confiée, parce que, pour nous, la mission est très sacrée. Alors, on pourra se sacrifier pour aller de l'avant. L'autosuffisance alimentaire au Burkina Faso nous allons l'atteindre », a assuré Oumou Koulsoum Baguian, VDP agricole de la commune de Bakata. Le coordonnateur de l’IP-P3A, Inoussa Ouédraogo, a assuré que ces jeunes sont prêts à mettre en pratique les connaissances qu'ils ont reçues. Les terres cultivables sont disponibles. Cependant, elles doivent être aménagées pour être pleinement opérationnelles. Il a saisi l'occasion pour inviter les bonnes volontés à soutenir cette initiative déployée au profit de la jeunesse burkinabè et du développement socio-économique. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : La Fondation Coris offre 360 tricycles aux VDP agricoles est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Benue police arrest 26 suspects, recover 495 rounds of ammunition
items.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Benue State Police Command has arrested 26 suspects, recovered 495 rounds of live ammunition and four locally fabricated firearms, and neutralised three suspected bandits in security operations across the state. The Commissioner of Police, CP Cletus Nwadiogbu, disclosed this on Tuesday during the command’s monthly press briefing in Makurdi. He said the operations also led to the recovery of 290 ammunition chains, the rescue of five kidnapped victims, and the recovery of a stolen Toyota Camry and a Honda motorcycle. Giving details of the operations, Nwadiogbu said operatives of Operation Zenda intercepted a vehicle travelling from Jato-Aka towards Makurdi through Gboko on November 15 and arrested a passenger, Timothy Shawon. According to him, 290 rounds of 7.62×51mm ammunition and 200 rounds of 7.62×39mm ammunition were allegedly found concealed in the suspect’s bag. He said further investigation led to the recovery of 290 ammunition chains, adding that the suspect was allegedly linked to the killing of security personnel at Agu Centre in September 2025. The commissioner also disclosed the arrest of two suspects, Michael Tyonongu and Godwin Agaibge, during a stop-and-search operation along Gbajimgba-Makurdi Road, where a locally fabricated pistol was recovered. In a separate operation, police arrested Dan Audu at Yagba community and recovered a locally fabricated revolver pistol and one live ammunition. Nwadiogbu said the suspect confessed to belonging to the Black Scorpion confraternity. On kidnapping, the police commissioner said five victims were rescued at Utange Village, Katsina-Ala, on November 8, but three died from injuries sustained during the incident, while two survived. He added that 10 suspects were arrested over the alleged abduction of a commercial driver, Mohammed Musa, a woman and her six-year-old son at Ojinebe-Adoka Village. According to him, the vehicle in which the victims were last seen was subsequently found burnt, while efforts to locate them were ongoing. The command also arrested two suspected armed robbers, Saviour Shagbaor and Maakaven Matthew, over an alleged attack on a commercial motorcyclist along the Gboko-North axis. Another suspect, Tersoo Orjime, was arrested in Makurdi, with a locally made revolver pistol and a knife recovered from him. Nwadiogbu further disclosed that three suspected bandits were neutralised during separate encounters with security operatives in Ukum Local Government Area. Items recovered during the operations included locally fabricated firearms, ammunition, cartridges, assorted charms and a stolen Honda motorcycle. The commissioner also said nine suspects were arrested over the alleged killing of 52-year-old Felix Ahemba in Gboko, while another nine were arrested over the burning of the Traditional Council Hall at Tyem-Imongu community in Vandeikya Local Government Area. He said the suspects arrested over the burning of the traditional council hall had been charged to court. In another development, operatives of Operation Zenda arrested Isaac Viashima in Gboko over alleged involvement in a criminal syndicate linked to armed robbery, kidnapping, fraud and ransom-taking. Nwadiogbu said two military uniforms, a dagger, desert boots and two rounds of ammunition were recovered from the suspect. Assessing the operations, the commissioner attributed the successes to intelligence-led policing, prompt response to distress calls, sustained patrols and collaboration with other security agencies. He urged residents to remain vigilant and provide credible information to security agencies, assuring that the command would sustain efforts to tackle criminal activities across the state. “We remain determined to identify, arrest, and bring offenders to justice, through lawful means,” he said. items.title: Cancer du col de l’utérus : vaccination et dépistage au cœur de la stratégie marocaine à l’horizon 2030
items.description: À l’occasion de la Journée mondiale pour l’élimination du cancer du col de l’utérus, célébrée le 17 novembre, le Maroc a lancé, mardi, une feuille de route nationale couvrant la période 2027-2030. Ce programme entend accélérer la vaccination contre le papillomavirus humain (HPV), élargir l’accès au dépistage et améliorer la prise en charge des femmes atteintes, avec pour ambition de faire de cette maladie évitable un problème de santé publique du passé. Le lancement de cette feuille de route marque une nouvelle étape dans la stratégie nationale de lutte contre les cancers. Présentée par le ministre de la santé et de la protection sociale, Younes Bjijou, elle s’inscrit dans la continuité du Plan national de prévention et de contrôle du cancer 2020-2029. Elle vise à renforcer les dispositifs existants et à inscrire le pays dans la dynamique mondiale d’élimination de cette maladie. « Nous disposons aujourd’hui de moyens efficaces pour le prendre en charge, le détecter précocement et même le prévenir bien avant son apparition », a souligné le ministre. La vaccination contre le HPV constitue le premier levier de cette stratégie, puisqu’elle permet de protéger les jeunes filles contre les infections à l’origine de la grande majorité des cancers du col de l’utérus. Le dépistage, notamment grâce au déploiement du test HPV et à la possibilité de l’auto-prélèvement, doit également faciliter l’accès des femmes à la prévention, en leur permettant de réaliser ces examens dans des conditions plus simples et respectueuses de leur intimité. Le troisième volet concerne la prise en charge thérapeutique. Le ministre a assuré que le Royaume disposait des compétences médicales et des infrastructures nécessaires pour accompagner les patientes et leur garantir des soins de qualité, dans des délais et des conditions adaptés. Un objectif mondial fondé sur trois cibles Cette initiative nationale s’inscrit dans le cadre de la stratégie mondiale lancée en 2020 par l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) pour accélérer l’élimination du cancer du col de l’utérus. Celle-ci repose sur les objectifs dits « 90-70-90 » : vacciner intégralement contre le HPV 90 % des filles avant l’âge de 15 ans, dépister 70 % des femmes à l’aide d’un test de haute performance avant 35 ans, puis à 45 ans, et assurer une prise en charge appropriée à 90 % des femmes présentant des lésions précancéreuses ou un cancer. Lors de la cérémonie, Dr Hafid Hachri, officier en charge du bureau de l’OMS au Maroc, a rappelé que le cancer du col de l’utérus demeure l’un des cancers les plus fréquents chez les femmes dans le monde et continue de provoquer chaque année des centaines de milliers de décès, principalement dans les pays à revenu faible et intermédiaire. Pourtant, a-t-il insisté, cette maladie figure parmi les rares cancers dont l’élimination en tant que problème de santé publique est désormais envisageable, grâce à des interventions dont l’efficacité est scientifiquement démontrée. « Pour la première fois dans l’histoire, nous disposons des outils nécessaires pour faire reculer durablement cette maladie », a-t-il déclaré, estimant que son élimination était désormais à portée de main. Le représentant de l’OMS a également salué les progrès accomplis par le Maroc au cours des dernières années, notamment en matière de dépistage, de renforcement des capacités diagnostiques et thérapeutiques et, plus récemment, d’introduction de la vaccination contre le HPV dans le Programme national d’immunisation. Autant d’avancées qui constituent, selon lui, des étapes importantes vers l’atteinte des objectifs internationaux. La question de l’équité d’accès aux soins Au-delà des dispositifs médicaux, les deux intervenants ont insisté sur la nécessité de réduire les inégalités d’accès à la prévention et aux traitements. Les obstacles financiers, géographiques et organisationnels ont longtemps limité le recours aux soins pour une partie de la population féminine. Le ministre a notamment mis en avant la généralisation de l’Assurance maladie obligatoire (AMO) et la réforme du système national de santé, présentées comme deux leviers destinés à alléger la charge financière des ménages, rapprocher les structures de soins des citoyennes et assurer une meilleure continuité des parcours médicaux. Cette transformation doit également s'appuyer sur les professionnels de santé, dont le rôle est central dans la prévention, le dépistage et l'accompagnement des patientes. La modernisation de leurs conditions de travail et le développement de leurs compétences figurent parmi les axes évoqués par le ministre, qui a également souligné l’importance du numérique, de la recherche scientifique et de l’innovation pour améliorer la compréhension de la maladie et orienter les politiques publiques. Pour Dr Hafid Hachri, l’enjeu est désormais de garantir que les progrès enregistrés bénéficient à toutes les femmes, sans distinction de lieu de résidence ou de situation socio-économique. « Chaque fille doit pouvoir bénéficier de la vaccination. Chaque femme doit avoir accès à un dépistage de qualité et à une prise en charge rapide lorsqu’une anomalie est détectée », a-t-il rappelé, soulignant qu’« aucune femme ne doit être laissée pour compte ». Un engagement qui dépasse le cadre sanitaire La lutte contre le cancer du col de l’utérus ne saurait toutefois se limiter à une réponse médicale. Le ministre a insisté sur les répercussions intimes, familiales et sociales de la maladie, ainsi que sur la nécessité d’assurer aux patientes un accompagnement respectueux de leur dignité et de leurs choix. Il a également appelé à une mobilisation dépassant les seules institutions sanitaires, en associant les familles, le monde éducatif, les médias, la société civile et les acteurs de proximité. « Vaincre le cancer du col de l’utérus dépasse le seul cadre médical », a-t-il souligné, plaidant pour une action collective et durable. La cérémonie a également été marquée par la signature d’une Charte nationale d’engagement, destinée à formaliser la mobilisation des différents partenaires autour de cette ambition. Pour le ministre, ce document constitue « un véritable pacte entre tous nos partenaires » en faveur de la protection de la santé et de la dignité des femmes. Younes Bjijou a, à cette occasion, salué l’engagement de la société civile, en rendant un hommage particulier à la Fondation Lalla Salma pour la prévention et le traitement des cancers, dont l’action aux côtés des pouvoirs publics se poursuit depuis plus de deux décennies. De son côté, le représentant de l’OMS a remercié l’Agence espagnole de coopération internationale pour le développement (AECID) pour son soutien à cette initiative, tout en réaffirmant la disponibilité de l’organisation à accompagner le Maroc dans la mise en œuvre de sa feuille de route, à travers un appui technique, le partage des bonnes pratiques internationales et le suivi des progrès réalisés. Si l’horizon 2030 constitue une échéance importante, l’ambition affichée dépasse cette date. Le gouvernement entend inscrire l’élimination du cancer du col de l’utérus dans une trajectoire nationale de long terme. « Ne laissons aucune femme payer de sa vie pour un cancer que nous savons aujourd’hui éviter », a lancé le ministre, résumant l’enjeu d’une stratégie qui entend faire de la prévention et de l’accès équitable aux soins les principaux instruments de ce combat. items.title: A.I.’s People-Pleasing Problem
New Nasarawa police chief warns against extortion
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The new Commissioner of Police in Nasarawa State, Sheikh Mohammed Danko, has warned officers and personnel against intimidation, extortion, unlawful detention and abuse of police authority. Danko, who has assumed duty as the 32nd commissioner of police in the state, said the police uniform represented a responsibility to serve the public and not a licence to operate above the law. He replaces Muhammed Shettima Jauro, who has been elevated to the rank of Assistant Inspector-General of Police. Addressing journalists at the command headquarters in Lafia, Danko said his administration would not tolerate corruption, excessive use of force, harassment or any misuse of police authority. He said: “Any officer found engaging in misconduct, political partisanship, corruption, or abuse of power will face immediate and appropriate disciplinary and legal actions.” The commissioner said complaints against police personnel would be treated seriously and thoroughly reviewed through the appropriate channels. He added that officers found culpable would be held accountable, irrespective of their positions, while personnel who discharged their duties honourably would receive the command’s support. Danko also cautioned political actors against using their offices or influence to intimidate citizens, provoke violence, obstruct lawful police duties or shield individuals from accountability. He directed officers to remain professional and non-partisan, warning against political pressure and private interests that could compromise their responsibilities. On security, the commissioner warned criminal elements involved in kidnapping, armed robbery, drug trafficking, cult-related activities and other violent crimes that the command would respond through intelligence-led and lawful operations. He also warned individuals providing shelter, weapons, information or other support to criminal networks that they could face the full weight of the law. Danko called for greater cooperation between the police and residents, urging community leaders, traditional institutions, youth groups and business owners to report suspicious activities through appropriate channels. He said public cooperation was essential to effective policing and reaffirmed the command’s commitment to protecting residents, enforcing the law impartially and strengthening public confidence across the state. The commissioner also advised residents against taking the law into their own hands or confronting suspects, warning that such actions could endanger lives and jeopardise investigations. items.title: Ebonyi demolishes shop over planning violations
items.description: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The Ebonyi State Government has demolished a shop on Ejiofor Street, Abakaliki, over alleged failure to obtain building plan approval and encroachment on designated land. The demolition was carried out by the Ministry of Capital City and Urban Planning. Speaking during the exercise, the Commissioner for Capital City and Urban Planning, Richard Ugo Idike, said the property owner commenced construction without obtaining the required building plan approval from the ministry. Idike explained that building plan approval was mandatory to enable the ministry assess proposed structures, conduct necessary inspections and provide professional guidance to ensure compliance with physical planning standards. He said securing approval before commencing construction would also allow the ministry to identify potential structural, environmental and planning concerns and advise property owners accordingly. The commissioner cautioned property owners and developers against unauthorised construction and encroachment on designated lands, warning that the state government would enforce relevant planning regulations against defaulters. Idike was accompanied during the exercise by the Head of the Town Planning Department, TPL Esther Nwite, other town planners and members of the ministry’s task force. He urged residents, developers and property owners in Abakaliki to obtain the necessary building plan approval from the ministry before embarking on construction projects. The commissioner reaffirmed the state government’s commitment to enforcing physical planning regulations and promoting orderly development in the state capital. The post Ebonyi demolishes shop over planning violations appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Seven former Alia Commissioners dump camp, back PDP’s Aondoakaa
items.description: …the only permanent thing in life is change – group leader By Peter Duru, Makurdi In a significant political development ahead of the 2027 Benue state governorship election, seven former commissioners who served under Governor Hyacinth Alia have declared their support for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Chief Michael Aondoakaa, SAN, pledging to work towards his emergence as the next governor of the state. According to a statement by the Director, Media and Communications for the Aondoakaa/Ogbenjuwa Campaign Organization, Dr. Terver Akase, the former commissioners announced their decision during a meeting with Aondoakaa, where they expressed confidence in his leadership experience, professional background and capacity to address the numerous challenges confronting Benue state. They described the former Attorney-General of the Federation as a leader with the requisite exposure and administrative experience to provide purposeful leadership and reposition the state for sustainable development. “The group pledged its commitment to mobilising support for Aondoakaa’s governorship ambition and expressed optimism about his ability to address critical issues affecting the state,” the statement said. Those who declared support for the PDP candidate include Prof. Moses Ogbaji, former Commissioner for Agriculture and Natural Resources; Mr. Aondowase Kunde, former Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management; Mr. Martins Shaagee, former Commissioner for Lands, Survey and Solid Minerals; and Mrs. Anna Itodo, former Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Welfare. Others were Joyce Luga, former Commissioner for Cooperative, Urban and Rural Development; Mr Omale Omale, former Commissioner for Power, Transport and Renewable Energy; and Matthew Aboh, former Commissioner for Information, Culture and Tourism. Responding, Aondoakaa expressed profound appreciation to the former commissioners for their decision to identify with his political aspiration, describing their support as “a demonstration of commitment to the collective interest of Benue State.” He noted that their decision to support his ambition went beyond personal interests, stressing the importance of putting the welfare and future of the state above individual and partisan considerations. The PDP governorship candidate assured the delegation that his administration, if elected, “will prioritise unity, security and inclusive development, with a clear commitment to bringing the people of Benue together.” He further outlined his development priorities, which included “tackling insecurity, creating employment opportunities, expanding infrastructure and strengthening critical sectors of the state’s economy and social development.” Aondoakaa maintained that “rebuilding Benue requires collective responsibility and the active participation of stakeholders across political, social and professional divides.” He emphasised that “the state’s progress would depend largely on the willingness of its leaders and citizens to put the common good above personal interests and political differences.” Contacted, leader of the group and former Commissioner for Lands, Survey and Solid Minerals, Martins Shaagee confirmed the development saying “the only permanent thing in life is change.” The post 2027: Seven former Alia Commissioners dump camp, back PDP’s Aondoakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tinubu approves Kebbi inland dry port, promises completion of landmark projects, improved security
items.description: ‎ ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ ‎ABUJA — PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu on Tuesday approved the full operationalisation of the Tsamiya Inland Dry Port in Kebbi, describing the facility as strategic towards boosting the state’s economy. ‎ ‎He also thanked the people of the state for their massive turnout and warm reception during the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally at the Haliru Abdu Multi Purpose Stadium in Birnin Kebbi. President Tinubu said he would not take their support and confidence for granted. ‎ ‎This is as former governors from the state have declared that they would work for President Tinubu’s re-election because he supported the state in times of need. ‎ ‎The former governors are Senator Adamu Aleiro, Sai’du Usman Nasamu Dankingari and Minister of Budget and Economic Planning Senator Atiku Bagudu. ‎ ‎At the campaign rally, the President reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to complete ongoing landmark infrastructure projects, especially the Illela-Badagry Superhighway, which passes through Kebbi, as well as other federal road networks within Kebbi State. ‎ ‎He commended Kebbi State Governor Comrade Dr Nasir Idris for complementing the federal government’s road-construction efforts and promised to expand the state’s agricultural programmes. ‎ ‎The President said: “We will expand the existing agricultural programmes. We will support rice mills in Birnin Kebbi, Argungu, Bagudo and Yauri. ‎ ‎” We will ensure that the Zuru–Rijau Road is actualised, while the Koko–Dabai road will soon be completed through the Kebbi State Government platform. We will rehabilitate the Goronyo–Argungu irrigation scheme and the Zauro Polder Project so that your farmers can farm year-round.” ‎ ‎On Security, President Tinubu pledged to strengthen further the national security architecture and support sub-nationals’ capacity to fight crime by signing the state police bill into law. ‎ ‎”We are mindful of the challenges in Zuru, Danko/Wasagu, Sakaba, Bagudo, Arewa, Shanga and some parts of Maiyama. We shall work together to end insecurity. ‎ ‎” In the meantime, we have deployed more troops to the state. We have provided more equipment to the military and police. We have approved new operating bases in Zuru, Bagudo and Yauri. ‎ ‎”By the grace of God, the days of bandits terrorising our innocent farmers are numbered, as we step up efforts to ensure that no farmer in Kebbi will be afraid to go to his farm again”, the President assured. ‎ ‎He further stated his administration’s determination to ensure peaceful elections while thanking APC leadership, supporters, and residents of Birnin Kebbi for their solidarity and impressive turnout. ‎ ‎In his remarks, Vice President Kashim Shettima reminded the audience of the support President Tinubu gave to late former President Muhammadu Buhari, enabling him to consolidate and win the 2015 presidential election. ‎He urged the northern voters to reciprocate the gesture. ‎ ‎The Vice President told the gathering that President Tinubu sacrificed his resources and comfort to give the North what it wished in 2015. He also thanked the North for giving the President 60.2% of the votes that gave the APC victory in 2023. ‎ ‎”The North repaid that kindness, and we are even more grateful that you are prepared to do the same in the coming election in January because you have rejected the lies, the distortions, the half-truths. ‎ ‎Earlier, the host Governor, Nasir Idris, commended the President for graciously approving his request to fully operationalise the Kebbi Inland Dry Port and other critical road projects in the state. ‎ ‎Gov. Idris assured the President of their support towards his re-election bid as a mark of appreciation for his support for the state’s socio-economic development. ‎ ‎The APC National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, commended some guests’ testimonies on President Tinubu’s commitment to infrastructure development in the country, especially in education, health, and security. ‎ ‎He assured the President that the North has resolved to support his re-election in 2027. ‎ ‎Senator AbdulAziz Yari, the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), thanked Kebbi residents for the massive turnout and commended the President for his massive investment in the state’s economy. ‎ ‎Yari urged Kebbi residents to come out en masse and vote for the President in the forthcoming 2027 Presidential general elections. ‎ ‎He said the creation of the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development was deliberate, aimed at addressing farmer-herder clashes in the north and supporting the ongoing construction of the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, designed to ease traffic along the corridor in line with the vision of Nigeria’s founding fathers. ‎ ‎Yari urged voters to disregard the deceitful voices of the opposition parties. ‎ ‎The Kebbi APC Presidential campaign rally was attended by First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu, Governors Uba Sani of Kaduna, Dauda Lawal of Zamfara, Mai Mala Buni of Yobe, Babagana Zulum of Borno and Ahmad Aliyu of Sokoto. ‎ ‎Others include Speaker of the House of Representatives Tajudeen Abbas; Senators Adams Oshiomhole and Ali Modu Sheriff; Minister of State for Budget and Economic Planning Doris Uzoka-Anite; Minister of Housing Muttaqha Darma; and former governors Ahmed Yerima of Zamfara, Ibrahim Shema of Katsina, and Abdullahi Ganduje. ‎ ‎The APC Campaign train has continued to criss-cross the country, engaging party stakeholders and Nigerians across the six geopolitical zones. The post Tinubu approves Kebbi inland dry port, promises completion of landmark projects, improved security appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: AFCON 2027Q: Late Oulai goal seals draw for Côte d’Ivoire against Gambia
items.description: Côte d’Ivoire denied Gambia an opportunity to go three points clear of Ghana following their draw game on Tuesday afternoon. Christ Inao Oulai came off trench to score a last ditch equaliser to salvage a point for the Ivorians in a 2-2 draw. Gambia came into the fixture looking to avenge the loss to Herve Reinhard’s side in matchday three of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers. However, it was Côte d’Ivoire who struck first in the game through Luc Zogbe, who was assisted by Amad Diallo. The away side held onto their lead from the 13th minute to go into the break with an advantage. Gambia made three changes at the start of the second half with one of them being involved in two goals after being introduced. Musa Barrow provided the assist for Yakub Minteh’s equaliser in the 69th minute before converting from the penalty spot 11 minutes later to hand Gambia the lead. The home side seemed well on course to claim all the maximum points but Oulai had other ideas. The Fiorentina midfielder found himself in a good position close to goal and fired the equaliser for the Group C leaders. The result on Tuesday blows open the group the final two round of matches to be played. Gambia maintain their second position, one point above the Black Stars who won both of their games against Somalia in Sekondi.

items.title: Humanitarian Coordinator calls for strengthened Ebola readiness in South Sudan
items.description: Country: South Sudan Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Juba, 17 November 2026 – The United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in South Sudan, Mr. Ramanathan Balakrishnan, has called for increased preparedness and readiness to respond to a potential Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the country. The call follows a recent full-scale simulation exercise conducted in October 2026 by the Ministry of Health, the National Public Health Institute (NPHI), the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners to assess the country's capacity to detect, notify, investigate and respond to a potential EVD outbreak. The exercise assessed key areas of South Sudan’s Ebola preparedness efforts, including case management, infection prevention and control, laboratory capacity, contact tracing and coordination. While the exercise demonstrated the system’s capacity to quickly detect simulated cases, significant gaps remain in alert management, rapid response team management, health worker remuneration, ambulance services, laboratory facilities, personal protective equipment supplies, contact tracing, and screening arrangements at points of entry. To address these challenges, the Humanitarian Coordinator has launched a three-month prioritised plan to mobilise financial resources to address the operational and capacity gaps identified during the simulation exercise. He called on donors and partners to support the plan, which requests USD$7 million to strengthen preparedness and response capacities. “While there are no reported cases of Ebola in South Sudan, closing these preparedness gaps is critical to ensure that South Sudan is better prepared to detect, contain and respond to a potential outbreak, and to protect the lives and well-being of its people,” Mr. Balakrishnan said. Reiterating the importance of national government leadership in strengthening EVD preparedness, Mr. Balakrishnan said, “The payment of health worker salaries by the government authorities is critical, as is facilitating access for Ebola-related movements for both health actors and UNMISS and ensuring the safety and security of humanitarian workers.”

items.title: CAN 2027, Togo – Algérie : le duo Hemdani – Antar Yahia sous pression
items.description: L’équipe d’Algérie attendra pour arracher sa qualification à la phase finale de la CAN 2027 après sa lourde défaite sur le score de 3-0 ce mardi à Lomé . Elle aurait pu se qualifier dès ce soir en cas de victoire à Lomé, mais les Eperviers ont dévoré les Fennecs pour se relancer dans la course à la qualification. Après cette victoire, ils sont remontés à la 2e place avec six points, une longueur de l'équipe nationale (1ère, 7 pts). Après trois victoires dont une en amical face au Niger, et un match nul, Brahim Hemdani concède sa première défaite depuis sa désignation surprise à la tête des Fennecs en septembre dernier en remplacement de Vladimir Petkovic. Passifs et sans âme, les Fennecs ont été dévorés des Eperviers plus entreprenants. Tout s’est joué en première mi-temps. Dominateur, le Togo ouvre le score dès la 18 e minute par Kindje qui fait le break peu après la demi-heure de jeu (32 e , 2-0). Quatre minutes, c’est Boateng qui saute plus haut qu’Abada pour fusiller le gardien Melvin Mastil d’une tête imparable. Trahi par sa défense, le gardien des Fennecs n’a rien pu faire. Le milieu de terrain des Fennecs, malgré la titularisation de Bentaleb, Abdelli et Titraoui, n’a pas pesé sur le cours du match. Passifs, les Fennecs marchaient parfois sur le terrain, au lieu de courir, laisser les Éperviers les dévorer, sans fournir aucune résistance. Togo – Algérie : les Verts prennent l’eau à Lomé En seconde période, Brahim Hemdani a tenté de reprendre la main sur le match, en faisant quelques changements, mais sans succès. Dans la possession de balle, l’Algérie a dominé, mais les autres statistiques ne sont pas en leur faveur. Le Togo a par exemple tiré 16 fois au but contre 8 pour les Verts. Les Eperviers ont cadré six tirs contre 3 pour leurs adversaires. Cette débâcle, qui survient après des prestations ternes malgré les victoires, relance le débat sur la capacité du duo Brahim Hemdani et son adjoint Antar Yahia à entraîner l’équipe nationale. En plus des choix discutables de certains joueurs qui évoluent dans des clubs presque inconnus, quelque chose échappe à ce staff technique qui multiplie les tâtonnements dans les compositions de l’équipe. Certes, il ne faut pas condamner Hemdani après une première défaite concédée face à une équipe aussi modeste que le Togo, mais les prestations des Fennecs suscitent des inquiétudes quant à leur capacité d’aller loin lors de la prochaine CAN 2027. Il semble qu’il manque de la rigueur et de l’engagement des Verts sur le terrain. L’article CAN 2027, Togo – Algérie : le duo Hemdani – Antar Yahia sous pression est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Over 170 major websites hit by attack, including BBC, Ikea and Air France: report
items.description: Nearly 200 major websites, including those of the BBC , HSBC UAE bank, Air France and Ikea were targeted by a malicious cyber attack seeking to steal financial information and infect Apple devices, specialist media reported on Tuesday. Hackers injected corrupted JavaScript code into tools hosted by Optimizely, a digital platform used by major companies to customise users’ online experiences, Cyber News reported, with some 178 websites targeted. “The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC , CNN , Salesforce, GitLab, Ikea, HSBC (UAE), Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock,” security researcher Scott Helme, who first uncovered the hack, wrote on Monday on his blog. “The attacker’s (crypto) wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th (of November).” Most of the malicious code had been removed from affected sites, Helme said in his post. Optimizely confirmed the incident and said it had identified “a security incident in which an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects”. It said it had fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code from affected projects, taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorised code from being delivered. “The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly,” it added on X. Bid to steal crypto, target iPhone users The websites were compromised in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, Helme said. According to the researcher, the scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker’s wallet. The malicious script also sought to capture payment card details as users entered them, steal cookies and screenshots, and deploy exploit code targeting Apple’s iOS devices, Helme said. Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock said it had also found evidence that the affected sites had served malicious code to visitors. Reuters could not immediately determine whether the malicious code had been successfully used in each case or the extent of any resulting compromises. Salesforce and Ikea said they were investigating the incident linked to Optimizely script changes. Salesforce said it had disabled scripts from the platform as a precaution. Equifax said it had immediately investigated the issue and stopped using the platform. “We have not identified evidence of any compromise to our systems,” it said. HSBC said unauthorised scripts were not active on its websites. Apple, Zoom and CNN did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The incident highlights growing risks facing organisations that rely on third-party software embedded in websites. Cryptocurrency hacks have resulted in more than $22.3 billion in stolen funds since 2021, according to blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis. Last month, a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3bn stolen from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance .

items.title: Long Wave
items.description: R uth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together. There is a big chest of drawers JP dragged home gleefully one evening, the scraping sound of her approaching, hollering for help. One of the other women, Sally, took it out into the concrete yard and sanded it down, repainted it, and then stenciled red flowers around the edges. As the women chopped carrots and argued about the rota, the children sneaked out at dusk and stuck their hands in the paint pot, left prints all over the front of the drawers. They get kids’ clothes from boxes on the street, charity sales and donations, and none of them fit right or they give way almost immediately at the seams but get shoved, nonetheless, into the chest of drawers and tugged out at random to put on whichever child needs them. Ori likes to go in by herself and dig thoughtfully through, chucking rejected dungarees and tie‑dye T‑shirts over her shoulder, plopping down on her backside to wrangle on leggings. Most of the swimsuits are nearly see-through from washing, the straps snapped, but Ruth manages to find enough and takes a handful of towels off the banister, puts them into the bag. The sun cream is out of date but will do the job. When she gets back into the sitting room, the cushions have been heaved off the sofa and everyone is bouncing on the wheezing springs. They have uncovered crushed breadsticks and molding apple cores but also a handful of lost 20-pence pieces, just enough for them all to get into the lido if she lies about some of their ages. She has been working all week, but today she is in charge. Ori rushes over and burbles something about jumping as high as the trees like a bird—no, like a dragon—and then tugs a pirate hat down as far as it will fit onto Ruth’s head. Let’s go, let’s go, she shouts, and everyone gathers, grabbing at shoes. There is Ori, who is 3—dressed this morning in a rainbow unicorn outfit with a wilting horn and a grubby tail—and Nora, with her shoes on the wrong feet, and Leo, who is 9 and an expert at making mayonnaise-and‑cheese sandwiches and wrapping them in foil. Last time they went to the lido he stole a rubber ring and he wears it slung around his middle now, hitching it up with one hand when it slithers down to his knees. There is also Bee, who is nearly 2 and who Ruth puts up on her hip to get out the door, and Tsembi, who is 7 and has a younger brother, Douglas, who bends to shit in his nappy beside the step, grunting intently. Sally has been making planters out of pallets to try to make some more money and they are stacked up outside the house with for sale signs pinned to them. Ruth and the kids make it down to the path and go in a ragtag, snaky line away from the house, Ruth yelling hold hands, hold hands, until everyone is pinned to someone else and trailing along. There isn’t enough cash for the bus. They’ll walk. Ruth hitches Bee onto her shoulders and Leo and Tsembi take turns carrying Douglas. The walk takes a long time. She changes Douglas’s nappy while the others climb onto the back of a bus-stop bench and compare war wounds. Douglas’s shit is runny and filled with little white worms again. It won’t be long before the others get them too. Ori is yelling loudly about being the fastest, fastest, fastest one and twisting back and forth to show off her scrapes and bumps, her multiple Moomin Band-Aids, which are grubby and starting to peel. Leo is hanging near her, his fingers beginning to tap a little in the way they do when everything is too loud and busy, his eyes glazing; Ruth calls him closer, tries to distract him, asks him to pass her cloths and then take the dirty nappy to a bin. Nora and Ori are arguing about who can stand on the back of the bench the longest without holding on. Bee is crouching and prodding at a snail nearby while Tsembi shouts at her to give it a rest, he’s only little, give it a rest. They make it to the pool. At the turnstile she counts heads and shoves the handful of coins in. They throw their towels down onto the brown grass and the kids strip their clothes off and fight over swimming costumes. She slathers sun cream on arms and legs and tries to stop Bee from falling in. Douglas examines his willy with his legs in the air and cries when a fat bee stings him on his round little belly. She scoops him up in one arm and gives him a sandwich. The older children are wading into the shallow end and lifting the water up in their hands and throwing it at one another, and Leo is dunking his head beneath the surface, where it must be good and quiet. Ori is leaping from the side over and over again, the force of her body leaving an after‑star‑shape in the air. Ruth gives Bee a sandwich too and puts on her own costume. It is one of JP’s and cuts in around the shoulders. Her mind is a rushing thing, trying to keep everyone in sight, tallying up who has sun cream on, thinking about what needs doing that day back at the house, thinking about the wood lice that have infested the room where she, JP, Leo, Nora and Ori sleep, which seem to dig their way up through the floors. There is a leak coming through the roof when it rains and sewage down the wall in the concrete yard whenever anyone upstairs flushes the chain. One night she woke, damp with sweat. JP was beside her on the blow‑up mattress and Leo and Nora were sprawled across the single beds, but when she looked again, Ori was not there. Ruth went out into the corridor. There was noise from the rooms above, which are rented out separately by students whom they almost never see, only hear. She had a sudden damp nightmare vision of Ori being spirited away or, rather, having never existed—she had never had a child. Sometimes, when she was pregnant, she had wished her away and now she was gone, she had never even been. She ran down the stairs. The front door was swinging wide and there was a white square of mucky moon and streetlight across the floor. Someone—one of the students—had left a half‑finished wine bottle on the front step. Ori was not in the yard among the stacked, unsold planters and experimental wooden birdhouses. A noise from the sitting room. Cheerios crunched under her feet. Ori was bent over in the corner, drawing with an imaginary pencil on the floor, talking quietly to herself. When Ruth pressed gently on her spine she sagged into Ruth’s arms, closed her eyes. That was the first time she walked in her sleep. The next day Ruth went and screamed at the hungover students, who came blearily out of their pizza-stinking rooms and scowled at her. Close the fucking front door, what is wrong with you? R uth tried everything to stop Ori from leaving the room at night. She tied her hands together by the wrists, she slept in front of the bedroom door, but always, somehow, Ori slipped free and Ruth would wake to her gone. It was a daytime and a nighttime problem. She was, JP said in exasperation after another desperate loudspeaker callout in the supermarket, a runner. Where had she gotten it from? This speedy, goat-like need to escape? Often, at the point of realizing she was lost, she would sit and wail. When they found her, she would be beside herself: You lost me, where were you? Ruth found herself thinking of the nights when the door of her childhood bedroom was locked against escape and she would knock on the walls and it would mean, I am here, I am here, are you there? One breakfast she undid the tie from JP’s dressing gown and rummaged around in the cupboard. The children were at the table, spoons hovering over their porridge, rumpled from sleep, watching her with suspicion. Ruth dug out a saucepan lid and tied it around Ori’s neck, gave her a metal spoon to bash it with. Ori’s eyes grew wide and she stood up on her chair. Bang , bang , bang , went the spoon on the saucepan, bang , bang , bang . That’s loud, JP said, holding closed her dressing gown. Well, we can hear where she is now, at least in the day, Ruth said. After that, Ori would often be given the saucepan lid or, if there was nothing else, stones from the ground or two sticks broken off a tree. JP started calling her Oystercatcher after the birds that hammer mussels and clams to try to get them open. At night, though, the sleepwalking continued and then began to get worse. On one bad occasion, Ori had made it all the way to the garden and was fiddling with the gate that led to the road when Ruth got to her. Ori was barefoot and tangle‑haired, moving fast. Ruth grabbed her, took her back inside, held her. Everyone was awake now, a bit upset, shifting around, Nora complaining, Leo singing quietly and tapping his fingers. Ruth, to try to calm them, began to tell the story of the knocking, not the wall one but the other. When you were in my belly, she said to Ori, I knocked and said, Hello, hello , and from the other side you knocked and said, I hear you, hello, how are you today? JP went out of the room and came back with the saucepan lid. She strung it—more, Ruth suspected, for comedic effect than anything else—around Ori’s neck, tied a wooden spoon to the edge of the lid. Just knock in your sleep, she said, and Nora and Leo howled and danced around, pretending to be sleepwalking, while Ori frowned thoughtfully, working out whether to be annoyed. Later, Ruth woke hard. A noise had come into her dreams and disturbed them. She had been dreaming about her mother in the kitchen of the house, she was wearing a green apron and stirring something in a large metal bowl and then she turned and looked straight at Ruth and said: Is someone at the door again? Ruth sat up. JP was already out of bed, crossing the room. She opened the door into the corridor. Past her Ruth could see Ori. She was sitting on the floor, cross‑legged, head bobbing to the sound as she struck the saucepan lid over and over and over. I hear you, JP said, I hear you, you’re here, don’t wake the whole house. S he takes the younger children into the water, floating them on their backs. She knows some of the other parents there a little; she also sees a few childminders with their own hordes of children, some serious swimmers in the main lanes plowing up and down, up and down. Leo gets Ori on his shoulders and ducks beneath the water and then explodes upward and she spins backwards and lands with a muffled boom and they do it again. Nora wants to show Ruth every one of the drowning beetles and wasps she is rescuing from the water. Douglas is mostly scared and clings on to her back like a splatted, soggy thing. They stay in for a few hours and then crawl out and lie on the grass under the sun. Some of the kids cry because they are tired and hungry. She feeds them sandwiches and they count out their coins and there are just enough for chips from the van. Leo comes back with a container and some ketchup. Ruth wraps Bee and Douglas and Ori in towels and lies down among them and sings them a song and they doze and wake and cry a bit and wipe their snotty noses on her arms and then sleep again. Ruth thinks Ori is sleeping but feels something on her cheeks and when she opens her eyes Ori’s face is directly above hers, nose to nose, water droplets falling from the strands of her straggly hair. Another of the women had given the kids haircuts, one after the other, bang , bang , bang , army‑style, and they are all bowl‑cutted now, spiky around the edges. Mama, come, Ori says, come on, Mama, up. She unravels herself from the other two and gets up and takes Ori’s hand. Leo is reading a book he has stolen from a sunbathing woman’s blanket. Tsembi is swimming a choppy doggy‑paddle up and down, copying the lane swimmers. Nora is digging for worms. Ori and Ruth investigate the bushes around the edge of the pool. There is a stretch of rubber tiles and an old, broken sprinkler system with rusted, sharp edges, and beyond that some giant overgrown wisteria. Ori has brought some worn plastic animals without Ruth noticing, a zebra with barely any stripes left, a polar bear without back legs. What do bears eat? Ori says, shoving the nose of the polar bear into the hardened ground. I don’t know. Honey? No. Silly Mama. Definitely not. I don’t know, then. Maybe fish? Yeah, maybe. Here’s a bear dance I just made up, she says, and jiggles and jaggles around, pushing her belly and her lips out and then sucking them in, sticking out her bottom. That’s cool, I like it. Yeah, maybe. Now you do it. Ruth tries to copy the dance exactly, waggling around. Not bad? she says. A bit bad, Ori says. A bit poo‑poo. She laughs and laughs. J P comes down after work and kicks off her shoes and sticks her feet in the pool. Ori flings her arms around JP’s neck and Nora and Leo show her the handstands they have been perfecting in the pool. The little ones have woken up and are back in the water. How’s it going? Ruth says to JP. Bouncing and bouncing and bouncing, JP says, bouncing motherfuckers, they need to stop bouncing and get a job. How’s it going in the madhouse? Fine, Ruth says, and tells her about worms and nappies. I’m so tired that I could sink into the water and sleep there, actually. Like a whale, JP says. Do you want to do a lap? Yeah, Ruth says. She leaves the children and goes to the adult side of the swimming pool. Her swimming costume is so thin, she thinks maybe everyone can see her bottom through it. She drops into the water. Some of the other women are wearing goggles and swim hats. She lets herself go down under the surface. It is not silent there but the noise comes wonky through the water and resounds bubbling through her. She swims along the floor with her belly scraping and then rises up and does a couple of lengths and then goes back to JP, who is yelling at Bee not to touch Douglas’s bottom if he tells her not to. She can tell, from looking at Leo, that he is overwhelmed by the noise and the argument. She sits beside him until he seems better and then she and JP lie in the last bit of the sun. The warmth feels good on Ruth’s closed eyelids. Look, JP says. When Ruth opens her eyes, JP is up on her elbows. Ruth levers herself upright. The children are playing a game. She hasn’t seen them play this one before. What is it? she says. Have you not seen this yet? Just watch. Nora has blindfolded herself with a towel wrapped around her head. All the children are there, on the grassy bit a little away from the pool, but Douglas isn’t really playing. They all have two stones, including Nora, whose stones are a little bigger than everyone else’s. They space themselves out. Blindfolded, Nora knocks her two stones against each other, tap , tap . The rest of them tap their stones together and Nora lurches forward, already laughing without making noise, and tries to get to them by figuring out where their taps came from. She nearly gets Leo because he is laughing so hard, but he skips out of the way and Nora has to stop and knock her stones together again. The rest of them, standing still, knock their stones together and the sound means: I am here . Nora comes for them. Ori darts away and then climbs up the metal fence and Nora knocks her stones together, asking, Where are you , where are you , and Ori knocks her stones together from the fence, I am here , I am here , and Nora comes and catches at her feet. They play for a long time, taking turns with the blindfold. A knocking game, Ruth says. Isn’t it good? Ori came up with it yesterday in the garden when I locked them out so I could make dinner. We should go, JP says. Yup, she says. They walk home the long way, carrying all of the children’s shoes in their hands. The children play a game involving trains chugging along a track. They stop briefly at a playground with a rusty red swing and a dirt groove beneath. The others like the slide, going down in a pile, seeing who can run down, but Ori likes the swing. She will stay on the swing for hours if they let her, clinging on to the metal chains, her torso tipped backwards, her chin rolled to the sky. JP and Ruth sit on a bench and talk about the child-care funding they had hoped was going to help them out but is less than half of what they thought it was going to be and whether they think the homeschooling is going okay. They talk about these things a lot and sometimes there are meetings in the house with the other women and with new women who come and go and mostly they all say: I don’t know what to do, I’m not sure. Sometimes the meetings are really good and people cry and talk and sometimes they all get annoyed and impatient and no one agrees and they just argue until they’re too tired to continue. Another meeting is scheduled for later that night after the kids are asleep. JP rolls her eyes and sticks out her tongue and says, I can’t talk about Sally quitting her job and making birdhouses anymore, she’s already bringing in hardly anything, and Douglas and Tsembi eat so much. Ruth laughs. Then they talk about what they want to say tonight. This is what I was going to say, shall I try it out on you? JP says. Go for it, Ruth says. Great. Hold on, she says, and they check on the children, count them, and Ruth looks for Leo, who listens to everything, and makes sure he is not close-up. Let’s go, everyone, they shout. They walk together along the road and JP holds Ruth’s hand. Well, I was going to say that I love them, obviously. I love all of them. I love Leo and Nora and I feel that I am the most lucky person to be their mum. I love Ori, I love that kid, did you know that? Yeah, Ruth says. I love their weird bodies and their silly sentences and I love that they were tiny and useless and now they’re just these crazy roommates. I was going to say all that but then I was going to say: I love them but I hate them. Oh yeah, that’s true, Ruth says. Like, what have they done to my life? Do they know that they are little bombs hidden under my floors and that they go off 10 times a day? Fifty times. A hundred and a thousand and a million times. They don’t know who I was before. I was a whole person. I was a child once and then I had a child and that child killed the child I was. That is insane. It’s insane. I was going to say something like that, JP says. What do you think? I think it sounds good, Ruth says. I think I’m going to say something like that too.

Adjei-Mensah Korsah calls for Rent Commissioner to be called to order over confrontational approach
items.description: Former Minister for Local Government, Decentralisation and Rural Development, Martin Adjei-Mensah Korsah, has criticised Rent Commissioner Frederick Opoku over videos showing him engaging property owners in what he described as near-violent confrontations. He said the approach adopted by the Rent Commissioner was unacceptable and could undermine efforts to address concerns over the high cost of accommodation, particularly for tertiary students. Mr Korsah argued that confrontational tactics were not a sustainable way of enforcing rent regulations, insisting that disputes involving landlords and tenants must be handled through established legal processes. “There are laws governing our rent regime in this country, and where they are flouted as it is believed to be the case, we must resort to the law,” he said. He further warned that the conduct of the Rent Commissioner, who acts on behalf of the government, risked creating an impression of lawlessness and impunity rather than promoting respect for the country’s legal framework. “A legal enforcement of these laws, in pursuit of fairness and Justice for our people, brings much more better results than the ‘Choooboi’ approach,” he added. Mr Korsah stressed that the use of force or intimidation in dealing with property owners could be dangerous and would not guarantee lasting solutions to the challenges confronting students and other tenants. The former Minister, who is the Ranking Member of Parliament’s Works and Housing Committee, made the comments in a Facebook post on Tuesday, November 17, calling for Mr Opoku to be called to order.

items.title: Le ministre Bouna parlant de la RSE dans les mines : «on peut prier chez soi, mais on ne peut pas étudier chez soi »
items.description: « On peut prier chez soi, mais on ne peut pas étudier chez soi. » C'est par cette formule que le ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, Bouna Sylla, a exprimé ses réserves sur certaines pratiques en matière de responsabilité sociétale des entreprises (RSE) dans le secteur minier guinéen. Interrogé en marge du Simandou Mining Summit (SMS), organisé à Conakry du 11 au 13 novembre, le ministre a plaidé pour une réorientation des investissements sociaux vers les infrastructures éducatives et les activités génératrices de revenus, tout en dénonçant les dérives constatées dans la gestion des Fonds de développement économique local (FODEL). Dans plusieurs localités abritant des activités extractives, la construction de mosquées figure parmi les réalisations sociales, alors que les besoins en infrastructures éducatives et économiques demeurent importants. Pour le ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, les investissements destinés aux communautés riveraines doivent avant tout répondre aux besoins prioritaires des populations et contribuer durablement à leur développement. Évoquant la gestion des ressources financières destinées aux collectivités minières, Bouna Sylla a notamment pris l'exemple de Télimélé, une préfecture concernée par l'exploitation de la bauxite. « Dans le cas de Télimélé, c'est 0,5 % du chiffre d'affaires des sociétés qui sont versés aux communautés directement impactées par l'activité minière », a-t-il expliqué. Cependant, le ministre estime que l'utilisation de ces ressources n'a pas toujours été conforme aux objectifs de développement local. « Mais l'expérience du passé a démontré que ces fonds ont plus servi à construire des mosquées ou à enrichir des gens », a-t-il dénoncé. Sans remettre en cause l'importance des lieux de culte, Bouna Sylla considère que les investissements sociaux doivent davantage privilégier des infrastructures indispensables à l'avenir des communautés, notamment les établissements scolaires. « Je suis musulman. On peut prier chez soi, mais on ne peut pas étudier chez soi », a-t-il souligné, pour insister sur la nécessité de privilégier la construction d’infrastructures scolaires. Selon lui, contrairement à la prière, qui peut être accomplie à domicile, l’enseignement nécessite des établissements adaptés pour accueillir les élèves et leur offrir de bonnes conditions d’apprentissage. À travers cette déclaration, il entend mettre l'accent sur la nécessité de mieux orienter les ressources issues de l'exploitation minière vers des réalisations ayant un impact direct et durable sur les conditions de vie des populations. Le FODEL, un instrument de développement à mieux encadrer Au-delà de la question des réalisations sociales des entreprises minières, Bouna Sylla a insisté sur la vocation du Fonds de développement économique local, alimenté par les contributions des sociétés minières au profit des communautés impactées. Selon lui, ce mécanisme doit permettre aux collectivités de financer des projets structurants, mais aussi de soutenir des initiatives économiques susceptibles de renforcer leur autonomie. « Le Fonds de développement économique local est dédié uniquement aux infrastructures sociales et au financement des activités génératrices de revenus au niveau des communautés locales pour rendre les communautés beaucoup plus autonomes », a-t-il rappelé. Le ministre a également reconnu que la gestion de ces fonds a connu des dysfonctionnements, nécessitant une intervention des pouvoirs publics. Pour y remédier, son département travaille en collaboration avec le ministère de l'Administration du Territoire afin de renforcer les mécanismes de gestion et de suivi des ressources destinées aux communautés minières. « Un travail de nettoyage est en cours par rapport à la gestion de ces fonds de développement locaux », a-t-il annoncé. Bouna Sylla fonde notamment ses espoirs sur la légitimité des exécutifs communaux, qu'il considère comme un facteur susceptible de faciliter la gestion des ressources et de renforcer la responsabilité des autorités locales. « Avec les exécutifs communaux aujourd'hui qui ont la légitimité nécessaire, élus par les communautés, l'exercice deviendra beaucoup plus facile. Mais il faut qu'il y ait une gestion transparente de ces revenus qui sont donnés à ces communautés-là », a-t-il insisté. Le ministre assure que les mesures engagées pour assainir la gestion du FODEL sont déjà bien avancées. « C'est le grand défi qu'on est en train de régler, mais quasiment terminé », a-t-il conclu.

items.title: Post-retirement contract: Haruna appeals to Mahama to guarantee automatic transition of academics
items.description: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has appealed to President John Mahama to ensure an automatic transition of university lecturers and other senior academics from age 60 to 65 under the post-retirement contract arrangement. He says the current transition process requires better coordination between the Ministry of Finance and the Controller and Accountant-General’s Department to prevent administrative delays that could disrupt academic work. Speaking during a meeting between President Mahama and the leadership of the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) at the Presidency on November 12, Haruna Iddrisu said the arrangement requires presidential intervention to guarantee a smooth transition for senior academics retained by universities. “The principle of automatic transition from that 60 to 65 would need your guidance and support for the Ministry of Finance and the Controlling Accountant General to commit to an automatic transition of those senior members and professors that are so desired by the university,” he appealed. He cited the example of a history professor who conducts examinations in July but turns 60 on August 30, questioning how such an academic would complete the process of submitting examination results under the current arrangement. Haruna Iddrisu also assured UTAG that the Mahama administration would respect the academic freedom of universities and would not interfere in their institutional independence. “Under your leadership, you have no intention, as President or through your ministers, to interfere with the academic freedom of any academic institution in Ghana,” he told the President. He said government’s focus was on providing the necessary infrastructure and support to improve the quality of education.
