items.title: Rs24bn additional QTA proposed by Discos draws protest from industrial consumers
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Industrial consumers on Tuesday protested over a Rs24 billion additional quarterly tariff burden proposed by power companies due to higher capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance (O&M) costs and the impact of system losses, resulting in an estimated tariff impact of around Rs1.30 per unit for three months. A brief intervention from the power division, represented by the chief financial officer (CFO) of the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), Naveed Qaisar, was the request at a public hearing that the additional quarterly tariff adjustment (QTA) be applied beginning in the Dec 1, 2026 billing and ending in February 2027. The hearing was presided over by National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) members Amina Ahmed, Maqsood Anwar Khan and Ghulamullah Shaikh, on the request of 11 distribution companies (Discos) to seek approval for charging the additional QTA for the July-September 2026 period. Once approved, the additional QTA would also be applicable to K-Electric under a government decision in place since 2023. Two industrial interveners — Amir Shaikh and Rehan Javed — expressed serious concern over Rs39bn additional capacity payment claims for the quarter against the pre-approved references built into the base tariff, besides the Rs5.6bn impact on variable O&M and Rs7.8bn impact of system losses in monthly fuel charges. Amir Shaikh, from Lahore, said QTAs normally stay negative when fuel cost adjustments (FCAs) are higher than charges to consumers in respective months. This time, however, the industry faced a double shock — positive FCAs throughout the quarter followed by positive QTAs — while the industrial output had gone out on the premise of lower QTAs. He said the major reason appeared to be units sold to selective consumers under the incremental consumption package (ICP) at an unrealistic cost of Rs10 cheaper than normal tariffs, which translated into a higher QTA for all consumers — despite the government’s promise that the impact of the ICP would not be charged to consumers except for ICP beneficiaries. “This is like rubbing salt into our wounds. It is shocking that the QTA has gone up,” he said. Javed, from Karachi, noted the Discos claimed Rs29.25bn of negative impact of the ICP on industrial consumers, saying it was actually an additional burden from all consumers. A series of questions he raised over the data provided by Discos remained unanswered and Nepra did not press for responses either. Javed alleged that the Discos had counted the wrong units and measured against FY2023-24, instead of references set for this year under the notified tariff. “The ‘relief’ shown (the ICP of Rs29.25bn) is not relief received; it hides a cost other consumers pay,” he said, adding that this was not legally covered by any Nepra decision as all consumers were being forced to fill a Rs15 per unit delta. He contended that when every Disco was claiming to have sold more units than the reference, the capacity cost should have reduced. “Why, then, is the capacity claim going up? Is the benefit of the higher sales being lost because of ICP units?” He demanded to defer the incremental units amount in the QTA claim until the full data, as demanded in March and September 2026, had been filed. Cumulatively, all 11 Discos reported that capacity charges during the July-September period had increased by Rs39bn, which also included the impact of system losses on the monthly fuel cost and variable operation and maintenance costs. Seven out of the 11 Discos demanded additional recovery of about Rs37bn on account of capacity charges, variable O&M charges and the impact of T&D losses on monthly FCA. However, a significant portion was offset by negative adjustments of Rs13bn from four other Discos. The highest additional claims came from Islamabad Electric (Rs10.833bn), followed by Rs10.46bn from Faisalabad and Rs7bn from Peshawar Electric. Tribal Electric led with a negative adjustment of Rs5.8bn, followed by Rs4.1bn by Quetta and Rs1.95bn by Hyderabad Electric. In line with policy guidelines issued by the federal government for uniform quarterly adjustments, the QTA determined for Discos for the third quarter of CY2026 will also apply to K-Electric consumers once Nepra issues its judgment. Under the tariff mechanism, changes in fuel cost are passed on to consumers only on a monthly basis through an automatic mechanism, while QTA, on account of variation in power purchase price, capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance costs, use of system charges and including the impact of transmission and distribution losses, is built into the base tariff by the federal government.

items.title: In hard-hitting speech, Bilawal says system was ‘made to collapse’
items.description: Key takeaways: Bilawal opposed creating new provinces ‘unconstitutionally’, such as via referendum ; urged PML-N to decide on provinces issue, claimed ‘ pressure ’ on PPP Called for releasing “political prisoners”, including Imran ; noted “ injustices ” to opposition regarding reserved seats, PTI symbol Said 27th Amendment passed without consensus ; supported Fazl’s “ right to criticise ” govt Amid debate on a “system reset” in the country, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said on Tuesday that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse”. Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”. During his speech at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal recalled Naqvi’s remarks and said, “Nobody objects that the system has collapsed, but there is no discussion and debate on why it collapsed.” He noted that the proposed solution “was not an actual remedy to the illness due to which we suffered a system collapse”. “If we want to focus on resolving the issues of the public, if we want to fight poverty, unemployment, inflation, then we absolutely need to decide why the system collapsed,” the Bhutto scion said. ’Reset must be political’ Bilawal asserted a reset was “definitely needed”; however, he also stressed that it should be political. “Why political? Because politicians are the representatives of the people, and if politicians do not play their role, then these fundamental issues won’t be resolved,” Bilawal said. “I believe the system has not collapsed, but it has been made to collapse,” he stated, while acknowledging his own role in the matter. “Everyone makes mistakes, but there comes a time when you must fix those mistakes. How do we fix that?” Bilawal asked rhetorically. He contended that state institutions had “lost their legitimacy”, calling for it to be restored. During his speech at the ‘Meet the Press’ event and responding to queries later, Bilawal firmly declared that the PPP would oppose any “unconstitutional” moves regarding new provinces. He also voiced his strong opposition to a referendum on creating new provinces, questioning the “intent” behind it, and said his party lawmakers were facing “pressure” but would not succumb to it. The PPP chairman’s remarks went beyond his oft-repeated calls for electoral reforms and political consensus, as he called for the opposition PTI to be given reserved seats as a “confidence-building measure”. He also questioned the current status of the judiciary, particularly in the wake of the 27th Amendment, which he had strongly advocated for at the time of its passage just a year ago. ‘Injustices’ to PTI of reserved seats, symbol The PPP chairman further observed that “some such injustices” had been done that, if corrected, could quickly restore the opposition’s trust. In an indirect reference to the PTI , Bilawal recalled the revocation of the PPP’s party symbol in 1988 and said, “Revoking the symbol from a party is akin to you joking with the public, and the public denounced this tradition and action and responded to you in those elections.” Then, in a stance deviating from the ruling coalition’s, Bilawal said that “what happened with the reserved seats was a joke”. He said the opposition was not only deprived of those seats, but “those in the treasury benches also put them in their pockets”. The PTI — deprived of its reserved seats in the 2024 elections — was declared eligible for the seats by the Supreme Court. However, a constitutional bench formed later via the 26th Amendment overturned that ruling while hearing review pleas of the coalition parties. “And from those same reserved seats, which are not yours, you brought constitutional amendments not once but twice, and are now thinking to bring a third one,” Bilawal said. He called for resolving reservations regarding rigging and returning the party symbol “so they have their own identity”. “It is a confidence-building measure that we, without any preconditions, return the reserved seats to the opposition, which is their right,” said Bilawal, whose PPP was also among the beneficiaries of the reserved seats case. ‘Imran Khan a political prisoner’ Reiterating his call for electoral reforms, Bilawal also stressed the need to restore the PTI’s and the opposition’s trust in the Parliament. “If we want the system to be reset and the Parliament to start functioning, vengeful actions will need to be stopped. How much revenge will you take after all?” he said. The PPP chairman said not only should vengeful actions be halted, but the “tradition of revenge inserted in Pakistan’s politics” should be ended forever. He even recalled a speech by PTI founder Imran Khan, who questioned if “we were ants”. Bilawal called for efforts to ensure that there is no political prisoner in Pakistan, terming it necessary for the “system to function”. “What a weird country this is; since 1947, whoever becomes the prime minister goes to jail, whoever gets out of jail goes to sit in the Prime Minister House,” he remarked. “You broke [our] back, then ask ‘why did you fall’,” he quipped, emphasising that political prisoners would need to be released. When asked whether he considered Imran a political prisoner, Bilawal responded in the affirmative. “A person becomes the prime minister and is later imprisoned. So I can either accept that every prime minister in the country’s history has been a thief, or I can accept that all prime ministers in our history have been victims of political revenge,” he added. Noting that the PTI had made mistakes as well, Bilawal said, “One day, I hope no prime minister should have to go to jail, and for that, we need to develop consensus.” ‘Federal govt must decide on reset’ Bilawal, in response to a question, also called on the federal government to present its stance on the governance reset. Presenting his own approach, he said, “The political reset that I spoke of, I will try to develop that consensus, and I would like to create a consensus for it in my own party so that we can engage other political parties”. As for the federal government, Bilawal said, “I don’t know what they are thinking.” In an apparent reference to the interior minister’s remarks about being on the “same page” as Bilawal, the PPP chairman said, “I had heard we were on the same page, and if this is the page we are on, then nothing could be better.” Bilawal said there had been a debate that had been “forced” in the country for the past few months. “Even the cabinet had not discussed the matter, let alone the parliament [..] So, how could it be that federal ministers are talking about it of their own accord,” he asked. At this, the PPP chairman said he would like to believe that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has “enough authority over his own ministers”. “You are sabotaging your own prime minister, and then you complain that the system has collapsed [..] I believe that is unfair.” In recent days, PML-N’s Khawaja Asif, who serves as the defence minister, has been advocating for new administrative units, suggesting the formation of up to 12 provinces. Bilawal maintained that his party would welcome any debate and consensus on the matter; however, he hinted that deliberation and consensus “may not be on the agenda”. Bilawal said that “suggestions” were coming from outside of the Parliament, which he described as showing “clear indication [..] that the opinion of Parliament, public, and cabinet did not hold any weight and you just want to use a backdoor channel”. “Up until today, neither the prime minister nor a single member of the provinces has brought up the issue with the president of Pakistan or me,” he added. On a possible rollback of the 18th Amendment, Bilawal pointed out that the Sindh government was giving the Centre Rs585 billion surplus in financial support. “Donations worth Rs 260bn were given in security and national interest,” he said. “I am not even counting the rightful share of the province — of petroleum levy and gas levy — it is about Rs1.7 trillion from the petroleum levy.” He remarked, “So, you will pickpocket the province, loot our resources and then come and ask us, ‘why the roads are broken and why no schools or hospitals have been built’.” Bilawal assailed the Centre, asking if a province was paying a Rs585bn surplus, Rs260bn for national security and Rs1.7tr on the petroleum levy, then “the federal government should be held responsible for the lack of public spending, not the provincial government”. He claimed that the “easiest way to do corruption in Pakistan was to be on the state’s right side”. ‘Referendum has never been democratic’ On the interior minister’s recommendation of holding a referendum to decide on the creation of administrative units, the PPP chairman pointed to the “intention” behind the proposed action. “In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one,” the Bhutto scion remarked. He argued that if the Constitution had relevant provisions on the creation of administrative units, then the mere suggestion of holding a referendum “meant that you were looking for an unconstitutional method”. The PPP chairman vowed that his party would stand firmly against any such “unconstitutional” action. Bilawal also spoke against “any forced division” in Sindh, warning that while PPP remained in favour of creating provinces, it was against a “forced separation”. He cautioned, “We talk about the garbage on Karachi’s streets, but if Sindh is divided, we will see blood flow through its streets.” On being asked whether a compromise could be reached on the creation of new provinces, Bilawal recalled that several resolutions had been passed by the Sindh Assembly against the province’s division. “Any more discussion on this issue is a slap to the people of Sindh,” he declared. “I do not understand what Mohsin bhai is trying to do,” Bilawal said. Replying to a question about new provinces and a “reset”, Bilawal said the PML-N-led government had not discussed the matter with the PPP, adding that this raised the question of why this was “being made to discuss by the media”. Bilawal said he has invited PM Shehbaz to hold talks with the Sindh government on public issues, and also suggested that he convene his cabinet meetings in each province. ‘Pressure on PPP lawmakers’ Reiterating the PPP’s stance on new provinces, Bilawal stressed that as a generational politician, he would want to take steps as per the public’s wishes. “Those from whom these suggestions are coming, they have not won even a single election in their lives. And neither do they have chances in the next election … they would become a minister, prime minister or chief minister whether they get a single vote or not in the next elections,” he said, adding that each side was taking a stance as per their situation. Replying to another query, Bilawal said, “On the one hand, there are no discussions ongoing; on the other hand, there definitely is pressure on the party’s MNAs and MPAs, but PPP’s representatives do not function on someone else’s pressure, but the public’s.” He further remarked, “If tomorrow, my software is updated and I direct my party to vote for Sindh’s division, there will be a revolt against me. They will not cast a majority vote even on my directives.” He quipped that “some people were dreaming of becoming the chief minister of their area, but they would not even be able to remain their house’s chief minister”. The Bhutto scion further affirmed that his PPP would not “back any conspiracy against Punjab”, adding that he would support only those decisions endorsed by the Punjab Assembly. He pointed out that there was a lack of discussion on declaring Gilgit-Baltistan a province even though there was a consensus in the region on this demand. ‘27th Amendment passed with brute majority’ Speaking on the judiciary, Bilawal noted that “our internal wish of a constitutional court” as per the Charter of Democracy had been fulfilled, but questioned whether the court had the public’s confidence. “If the lawyers and judges themselves do not have confidence in the courts, then the system did not collapse, but was made to collapse.” The PPP chairman said he was not calling for the revocation of such moves, but for greater consensus. He asserted that the 26th Amendment was passed with “bilateral agreement, if not complete consensus”, as the opposition’s input was taken through Fazl. Bilawal said the 27th Amendment was “passed neither through political consensus nor bilateral agreement; it was passed with brute majority”. He called for engaging with the opposition on judicial reforms and termed it a requirement for the “political, public and democratic reset”, adding that without such a reset, the public’s key issues of inflation and unemployment cannot be addressed. Bilawal also noted that rigging allegations often surfaced during elections. “I have been in politics for the past 20 years, and usually, I have seen that it is the opposition that accuses the other side of rigging and the government denies it. For the first time, I am seeing that people from within the government are claiming that rigging has been done.” ‘Fazl has right to criticise govt’ Bilawal also came to Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s defence as tensions between the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief and the government have flared in recent weeks. The past month has witnessed exchanges of harsh remarks between Fazl and federal ministers, after the JUI-F chief accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights. These developments came after Fazl joined the opposition in criticising the Centre’s imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the PTI-ruled KP. He also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the federal and KP governments. In his address, Bilawal stressed that it was the opposition’s role in the Parliament to criticise the government. “It is the opposition’s right to criticise you, and however he (Fazl) does it, it is their right,” he said. Bilawal remarked that the opposition had the “most patriotic” role in the Parliament. “For any government to question the patriotism of an opposition member [..] it is not only an injustice to that parliament or to the system, but the biggest injustice to the country,” he added. The PPP chairman termed a difference of opinion within the Parliament the “beauty and strength of democracy”. Bilawal reiterated, “If we want to reset the system, a political reset has to happen; it should begin from the parliament”. He noted that the opposition had lost trust in the system. “They genuinely have reasons to have lost confidence in the working of the Parliament, and we all have to regain this trust,” he said. “The government cannot expect the opposition to clap along with every one of the government’s decisions,” he remarked. He claimed that the “easiest way to do corruption in Pakistan was to be on the state’s right side”. Bilawal said: “When someone from the opposition makes a speech [..] then all of a sudden, you set the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) on them, arrest their sons; there was no such realisation before. “Now, all of a sudden, there is encroachment (around their house),” he said, in an apparent reference to the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) recent notice on “unauthorised construction” at the JUI-F chief’s residence. “This is why the system has collapsed […] you are making it collapse,” he said, calling on the Centre to engage with Fazl. On governor’s rule in KP, Bilawal noted that PPP had the governor in the province, but stressed his stance that it could not remain forever. “If you are yourself saying that the majority of them (PTI) were ready but one or two people sabotaged the talks, then what is stopping the government from approaching the opposition again?” he said, recalling remarks by “minister for everything”. “If the PTI is ready to fight against terrorism together with you, then the governor’s rule can also be ended,” Bilawal said, terming it another way to regain the opposition’s trust.

items.title: Projet urbain skills : l’ANPEJ cible 600 jeunes dans les métiers de mobilité urbaine à Sédhiou
items.description: Dans une perspective de lutte contre le sous-emploi et d'offrir à la jeunesse des possibilités d'insertion, l'ANPEJ cible 600 jeunes pour les outiller dans des métiers de la mobilité urbaine à travers la région de Sédhiou. Sédhiou – C'est autour de la région de Sédhiou d'accueillir, ce mardi 17 novembre, l'Agence nationale pour la promotion de l’emploi des jeunes (ANPEJ) dans le cadre de sa tournée d'information sur le projet Urban Skills, une initiative qui vise, à en croire Lamine Thiam, responsable du projet, à former et à insérer 600 jeunes dans le secteur de la mobilité urbaine durable. Selon toujours M. Thiam, ce projet permet de former les jeunes sur les métiers prioritaires comme la maintenance des véhicules électriques, la maintenance et la réparation des bornes de recharge, l'assistance aux voyageurs, entre autres métiers identifiés dans le secteur de la mobilité urbaine. A lire aussi : Transport : Salif Mané élu à la tête de la gare routière de Sédhiou Mis en œuvre par l'Agence universitaire de la Francophonie en collaboration avec l'ISEP de Thiès, l'ANPEJ, la SETER et Dakar Mobilité, le projet Urban Skills est financé par l'Union européenne et la coopération allemande. Il a démarré en septembre 2025, avec une enveloppe de moins de deux millions d'euros. Il doit durer deux années. Dans le processus de recrutement des futurs candidats, des critères de sélection sont élaborés. « L'admission concerne les jeunes jusqu'à l'âge de 35 ans. Un quota est prévu pour les adultes, aussi bien pour les personnes en situation de handicap que les migrants de retour », a expliqué de son côté Mbaye Diaw, point focal du projet Urban Skills à l'Agence nationale pour la promotion de l’emploi des jeunes (ANPEJ). « Les candidats devront avoir une préqualification, ils vont recevoir une formation de six mois dont trois mois en présentiel à Thiès et deux mois de stage, avant de finir à la suite d'une période de certification à l'issue de laquelle ils obtiennent un certificat d'aptitude professionnelle », complète Lamine Thiam, à la tête du projet. La rencontre de Sédhiou est la douzième étape depuis le lancement du projet. « Nous venons de lancer la ligne directrice pour le recrutement des futurs bénéficiaires, nous lançons un appel à la jeunesse pour qu'elle vienne s'inscrire massivement », a déclaré M. Thiam. Jonas Souloubany BASSENE (correspondant)

items.title: Éducation au climat : la Cosydep préconise une approche holistique
items.description: La coalition des organisations en synergie pour la défense de l’éducation publique (Cosydep) a organisé le mardi 17 novembre 2026, à Dakar un atelier d’une journée consacré au dialogue politique sur les Nexus éducation-climat au Sénégal. Autrement dit, intégrer la question du climat dans les enseignements/apprentissages et dans les politiques publiques. L’atelier tenu le mardi 17 novembre 2026, à Dakar sous l’égide de la Cosydep, a pour objectif de renforcer le dialogue et la concertation entre les institutions publiques, les organisations de la société civile et les partenaires techniques et financiers autour du nexus éducation-climat ; il s’est agi également de formaliser les engagements concrets en faveur de l’intégration de l’éducation dans les politiques climatiques et, réciproquement, de la prise en compte des enjeux climatiques dans les politiques éducatives. La rencontre présidée par le ministre de l’Éducation nationale a réuni une quarantaine de participants, délégués par les organisations syndicales d’enseignants, de la société civile, des groupes des partenaires techniques et financiers, ainsi que ceux des ministères de l’Éducation, de la Formation professionnelle et technique, de l’Environnement et du Développement durable. Les communications des différents acteurs ont permis d’avoir une idée nette sur la démarche et le niveau de prise en charge de la question de l’adaptation au climat. Selon Cheikh Tidiane Aw, chargé de programme à la Cosydep, il est constaté que sur le terrain, les acteurs ne travaillent pas en synergie, et pour pouvoir avoir des réponses vraiment viables et durables, il faut que les secteurs communiquent pour trouver des réponses par rapport aux défis climatiques. A lire aussi : Fawe Sénégal sensibilise par une randonnée pédestre « C’est pourquoi aujourd'hui, nous avons organisé cet atelier d'abord pour institutionnaliser l'approche, que ce soit une approche holistique, mais également pour que les acteurs puissent s'engager aujourd'hui, que ce soit l'environnement, l’éducation, à prendre en compte les questions climatiques dans leur politique. Et dans ce contexte de refondation du système éducatif, nous souhaitons faire des contributions pour alimenter cette refondation de l’école. L’école est à la fois victime et solution aux changements climatiques car l'école doit trouver les réponses auxquelles les communautés sont confrontées. Donc, c'est un levier qui est malheureusement négligé et nous souhaitons repositionner ce levier pour que l'école soit au centre vraiment des réponses aux défis climatiques », souligne Cheikh Aw, chargé de programme à la Cosydep. À l’en croire, le changement climatique peut impacter la qualité des enseignements et le quantum horaire, avec les effets des inondations, la canicule et la destruction des infrastructures et ouvrages scolaires. Ce qui, à son avis, favorise le décrochage scolaire. Venu présider la cérémonie d’ouverture, le ministre de l’Éducation nationale a salué la pertinence de la thématique et déplore la faiblesse du niveau de prise en compte de l’environnement dans les programmes scolaires. Moustapha Mamba Guirassy rassure tout de même que dans le cadre de la refondation du système éducatif et la mise en œuvre de la nouvelle initiative pour la transformation humaniste de l’éducation (Nithé), l’éducation environnementale de manière générale. « J'invite les acteurs ici présents à fédérer les synergies et vous verrez que nous aurons un impact extrêmement fort sur les changements de comportement lorsqu'on sait pourquoi respecter un arbre, pourquoi respecter son environnement, lorsqu'on arrive à l'intégrer dans son environnement, à se l'approprier, les choses vont changer », assure le ministre Moustapha Mamba Guirassy. Pape Coly NGOME

items.title: Pakistan’s pace trio routs Sri Lanka for 98 before hosts take control
items.description: Pakistan’s fast bowlers dismissed Sri Lanka for a paltry 98 before the home side reached 121-3 on the opening day of the second Test at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday, taking a 23-run lead into the close of play. Mohammad Abbas, Razaullah and Aamer Jamal claimed three wickets apiece as Sri Lanka were bowled out in 35.3 overs after Pakistan won the toss and elected to field on a green-tinged pitch. The visitors’ innings was the lowest total by any team at the venue, surpassing England’s 112 there last year. Pakistan’s reply was built around an 80-run opening partnership between Tayyab Arif and Azan Awais. Tayyab made 46 before the visitors struck back in the final session, removing three wickets. Awais remained unbeaten on 47 at stumps, alongside nightwatchman Saqib Khan, who was on two. The day had begun with Sri Lanka struggling to cope with Pakistan’s pace and movement. Saqib, who took seven wickets on debut in the drawn first Test, made the early breakthrough in the fourth over, drawing an edge from Pasindu Sooriyabandara, who made two, for wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori to take the catch. Abbas then removed the experienced Dinesh Chandimal, caught at short leg by Awais for seven, before Kamindu Mendis edged to Tayyab at short cover for eight. Sri Lanka were 25-3 and under mounting pressure. Razaullah made further inroads to leave the visitors reeling at 36-5. Opener Lahiru Udara, who had laboured for 34 balls to make four, was caught by Mohammad Taha at first slip, while first-Test centurion Dhananjaya de Silva was trapped leg-before for one. Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha offered the only meaningful resistance, adding 49 for the sixth wicket to give the innings some substance. Kusal top-scored with 32 from 50 balls, hitting five fours, while Dinusha made 21 from 40 deliveries with four boundaries. The partnership was ended by Jamal, who dismissed Kusal with a short delivery that produced a miscued hook. Dinusha fell to the same bowler in similar fashion, pulling a short ball to a fielder in the deep. Their departures triggered another collapse, with Sri Lanka losing their last four wickets for just 13 runs. Razaullah bowled Milan Rathnayake without scoring, Abbas took a return catch to dismiss Prabath Jayasuriya for three, and Jamal completed the innings by removing Lahiru Kumara. Abbas finished with 3-14, Razaullah took 3-21 and Jamal returned 3-24, while Saqib claimed the other wicket. Pakistan’s openers initially had to negotiate movement from the new ball, with Rathnayake particularly disciplined in keeping them quiet. But Tayyab and Awais settled in and gradually found their scoring rhythm, putting together an 80-run stand that gave the hosts a strong start in pursuit of Sri Lanka’s modest total. Tayyab was the more fluent of the two, finding boundaries with confident strokeplay, while Awais also began to open up as the innings progressed. Their partnership put Pakistan in a commanding position before Sri Lanka found a way back in the final session. Spinner Prabath Jayasuriya broke the stand by dismissing Taha for eight. Captain Babar Azam then fell for the same score, bowled by Lahiru Kumara after leaving a delivery that went on to hit the stumps. Awais, however, remained at the crease to guide Pakistan beyond Sri Lanka’s total. With the hosts on 121-3 when bad light brought play to an end, he was unbeaten on 47, while Saqib had joined him at the other end. Sri Lanka bowling coach Ryan van Niekerk described the first-innings collapse as a shock, saying his side had not expected to be dismissed for fewer than 100 in a Test. He said the priority was to fight back with attacking bowling and take early wickets on the second morning, adding that claiming four wickets in a session would be a positive response. Jamal praised the surface for offering assistance to the fast bowlers and said Pakistan had made the most of winning the toss. He remained confident that the hosts could build a substantial lead despite losing three wickets. The first Test of the two-match series ended in a draw. Tuesday also brought a setback for both teams in the World Test Championship, as they were fined and docked points for slow over-rates. Sri Lanka lost 15 points, slipping from seventh to eighth in the nine-team standings, while Pakistan were deducted five points after falling five overs short. They remained ninth and last.

items.title: Autonomisation économique des femmes : l’accès aux ressources, un défi dans l’espace UEMOA
items.description: L’accès sécurisé à la terre, aux financements et aux technologies demeure une difficulté majeure pour les femmes dans les pays de l’Union économique et monétaire ouest-africaine (UEMOA). Réunis lors d’une rencontre organisée à Saly ce mardi par le ministère de la Famille, de l’Action sociale et de la Solidarité, les participants ont partagé leurs expériences afin d’identifier des réponses communes à ces obstacles. MBOUR – Les obstacles à l’autonomisation économique des femmes restent largement partagés dans l’espace UEMOA. Malgré les efforts engagés dans les différents États, l’accès à la propriété foncière, aux ressources financières et aux outils technologiques continue de se heurter à des contraintes sociales, économiques et institutionnelles. C’est autour de ces préoccupations que s’est tenue à Saly ce mardi une rencontre consacrée à la restitution de la feuille de route de l’UEMOA. L’initiative a permis aux représentants des huit pays membres de confronter leurs expériences, d’examiner les difficultés rencontrées sur le terrain et de dégager des pistes d’amélioration. Pour Dr Nancy Ndour, directrice de l’Autonomisation et de la Femme au ministère de la Famille, de l’Action sociale et de la Solidarité, l’objectif est de favoriser une dynamique communautaire autour de l’accès des femmes aux ressources productives. « Il s’agissait de partager les expériences et la feuille de route de l’UEMOA en matière d’accès au foncier sécurisé, au financement et à la technologie pour les femmes », a-t-elle précisé. Ainsi, la question foncière occupe une place centrale dans les discussions. Dans plusieurs communautés, les traditions et les pratiques sociales continuent de limiter les possibilités pour les femmes d'accéder à la propriété ou d'hériter des terres. Une situation qui fragilise leur autonomie économique et réduit leurs capacités à développer des activités productives. A lire aussi : JOJ Dakar 2026 : Ngaparou, Saly et Malicounda se mettent au vert « Les femmes ont des problèmes d’accès au foncier parce que, d’habitude, sur le plan culturel, on nous dit que la femme ne doit pas hériter », a souligné la Dre Nancy Ndour. En plus, les difficultés ne se limitent toutefois pas à la terre. L’accès au financement constitue également un obstacle important, notamment en raison des conditions imposées par les circuits financiers classiques. Les taux d’intérêt élevés rendent souvent les crédits difficilement accessibles aux femmes entrepreneures et aux organisations féminines. À cela s’ajoute le déficit d’accès aux technologies, notamment aux outils de communication et aux solutions numériques adaptées à leurs besoins. Les travaux ont révélé que ces contraintes présentent de nombreuses similitudes dans les huit pays de l’Union. Si des différences existent dans les dispositifs juridiques nationaux, le Togo apparaît notamment comme l’un des pays ayant enregistré des avancées importantes sur le plan législatif. Le Sénégal entend également renforcer son cadre d’intervention avec la loi d’orientation sur l’autonomisation économique de la femme, dont le projet a été adopté en Conseil des ministres le 10 septembre 2025. Ibrahima MBAYE (correspondant)

items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived a congressional impeachment attempt last week, but oversight of Hegseth will be one of the new Congress’s most pressing tasks. Though Hegseth’s management of the war in Iran—a war that has now passed its eighth month without a constitutionally mandated congressional declaration—is his most glaring failure, the politicization of the Pentagon, the purging of qualified generals, and the targeted, extrajudicial killing of noncombatants all demand investigation and debate. In this episode of Autocracy in America , Representative Jason Crow talks about what form congressional oversight of the military should take. Crow sits on the House’s Armed Services and Intelligence Committees. The following is a transcript of the episode: Anne Applebaum: I’m Anne Applebaum. In this season of the Autocracy in America podcast, we’re asking how to undo the damage the Trump presidencies have now done to our political system, and how to reverse the slide to autocracy, even as Trump himself remains in office. In modern times, no U.S. president has politicized and personalized the military more than Donald Trump. During his first term, he told his then chief of staff, John Kelly, that he wanted to have the kind of generals that Hitler had, who would be totally loyal to him and follow orders. This instinct directly contradicts the ethos of the U.S. military, whose officers are trained to be loyal to the American Constitution and not to a particular politician or party. In his second term, Trump has done his best to establish a more autocratic ethos inside the military. He appointed Pete Hegseth, a Fox News host with no major organizational experience, to be secretary of defense. Hegseth, using opaque, informal criteria, immediately began firing qualified, experienced senior military leaders who just happened to be female or Black. He then continued to purge respected, talented officers, often with no public explanation. Since January 2025, Trump and Hegseth have taken the U.S. military even farther away from their traditions. They ordered strikes on fishing boats allegedly carrying drugs, a form of extrajudicial murder. They launched a war on Iran unprovoked, causing civilian casualties and damaging U.S. bases in the Gulf to a degree that has still not been fully accounted for or explained to the public. Trump even involved the Pentagon in a murky transaction in Venezuela, drawing the military into what may be a corrupt relationship with the Chavista regime, now led by Delcy Rodríguez. To talk about Trump’s attempt to transform the culture of the U.S. military into something recognizably autocratic, I’ve invited Jason Crow, congressman from Colorado. Congressman Crow is a veteran of the 82nd Airborne Division and the 75th Ranger Regiment, and he fought in Iraq and Afghanistan. [ Music ] He serves on both intelligence and armed services committees in the House and will be one of those investigating the abuse of the military. Congressman Jason Crow, thanks for joining us. Jason Crow: Thank you, Anne. Applebaum: We’ve already had one failed attempt to impeach Pete Hegseth. Will there be another? And why does it matter? What do you think impeachment can achieve? Crow: Yeah, it’s a great question, Anne, about: Are we gonna impeach Hegseth? And I remind folks that impeachment is just a tool. It’s not an end in and of itself, right? It’s a tool. There are many tools Congress has available to achieve its goals. So we actually have to start with: What is the goal? And the goal, for me, is to get Pete Hegseth removed as the head of the Department of Defense. Because every day he sits atop the DOD is a day that our service members don’t have the leadership, they don’t have the competency, they don’t have the direction and the support that they need, and they are being put at great risk. So removing Hegseth is the goal. Impeachment is one of the ways to do that, and I won’t hesitate to pursue impeachment if I think it’s the way to achieve that. Applebaum: But will the impeachment process address some of the deeper harms that he’s done? For example, the politicization of the military—the fact that Hegseth fired or removed very senior generals and commanders apparently for reasons that had nothing to do with merit, that were to do with whether they were so-called DEI hires, whether they were Black, whether they were women. Is there any way to fix or go back or reexamine any of that? Crow: You don’t fix those things via impeachment. You can discover those things in an impeachment investigation, in an impeachment proceeding and trial, of which I am very familiar ’cause I was an impeachment prosecutor in the first impeachment of Donald Trump, so I know a lot about the process. There is a fact-finding, investigative aspect of impeachment, and then that goes for ultimate—a trial for conviction in the Senate. But you don’t fix those things through impeachment. So we’re gonna embark on an investigative and fact-finding process. We have created, under the Armed Services Committee—or we’re about to create; we’ve already publicized this—a new subcommittee called the Oversight and Investigation Subcommittee, where we’re gonna put a lot of the investigations into that subcommittee, and we’re gonna start that in January. And then in addition to that, our other subcommittees of jurisdiction—the personnel, the readiness, the tactical land and sea forces—those are all gonna do their own investigations. The point is not just to do an investigation. The point, Anne, per your question, is to actually discover the information, because the last two years, our ability to get information has fallen off a cliff. They have stonewalled; they have refused to answer; they’ve refused to brief us. There’s so many things we don’t know that we have to learn. Applebaum: Let me also ask what you and your committee, and Congress more broadly, can do about stopping or forcing a negotiation to end the war in Iran. I know there are some deeper issues about whether the president defied Congress to start it. Will Congress have the ability to change how it’s fought? Will we learn more about the damage done to U.S. bases and U.S. interests in the region? Crow: Well, we’ve now taken votes, and these are in the form of resolutions to end the war in Iran. So we actually have a standing resolution that has passed that says that the president must end the war. And when we retake the majority, we will have more options to look at how do we enforce that resolution. But the more powerful tool, and probably the more viable tool, is funding. We can just cut the funding off, and I do not buy this argument at all that when you break it, you buy it—that we just have to continue to throw good money after bad. That’s what we did for years in Iraq and Afghanistan. We heard some variation of this argument: that we have to continue to do it, because one more troop surge, one more new strategy, one new general or admiral with a new idea about how to prosecute the war is somehow gonna fix it. Or, you know, escalation is the way out. We spent $3 trillion, 7,000 American lives, hundreds of thousands of lives wounded. We want out. Americans want out. That was the message last Tuesday. They don’t want this endless cycle of conflict anymore. So yeah, we can cut it off and direct the military to wind down operations, and that’s my intent. Applebaum: And so you would just say in a budget resolution, “We don’t fund this,” and then the money doesn’t go. Is it that simple and that straightforward? Crow: It’s not as straightforward as that. We have an appropriations process that we’re starting in January, so a budgeting process. We have to look at the ongoing budget. How do we detract money from those functions, right? So you have to figure out, and this is part of the fact-finding process and why fact-finding is so important, because: How are you paying for this? What units are deploying and when? Those are all the essential questions we have to ask and the answers we need to get, so then we can figure out: How do we budget that to make sure that we are peeling out the critical national security functions that have to happen, that have to continue, and we’re not impacting those operations, but we are properly carving out Iran war operations and winding down that funding? Applebaum: And will this process begin to return power to Congress over warfare, which is what Congress is meant to have? Crow: It’s a great first step, right? I think the story of the moment we’ve been in the last two years is a story of the height of presidential power in America and the low point of congressional power in American history. We have to correct that, and it starts with appropriations in January, but we also have to revisit the authorizations for use of military force, these AUMFs that are being used as blank checks now for military operations. And that’s not to say that we shouldn’t use the military to keep ourselves safe, to combat terrorism, to support our allies. That’s not what I’m saying. But what I am saying is these AUMFs that have been on the books for over 20 years now without debate, without reauthorization, and without appropriation. They’re funded largely by debt funding at this point. They have to end. And no Congress should occur—there shouldn’t be any two-year period where the people’s elected representatives aren’t forced to debate and vote on these. Applebaum: Let me now turn to a slightly different subject but one that’s related, which is the military’s attacks on fishing boats allegedly carrying drugs. These were attacks that you could describe as extrajudicial murder: using the military to attack civilian targets. Maybe they were carrying drugs. Maybe they weren’t. There was no process to find out. People were killed, and famously on one occasion, people may even have been killed by a second strike—survivors of a first strike—by an American missile or an American bomb. Is that something that Congress can force the military to take responsibility for? Is it something that we can hold them accountable for? Crow: Absolutely, and it’s near the top of my list. I’ve heard some people say these are war crimes. There’s no war. There’s no declaration of war— Applebaum : Exactly. Crow : —so they’re not war crimes, which actually just makes these, if they are what they appear to be, murder. If there’s no war, and you have no self-defense argument—which in some of these cases is very clear to me. I’ve actually seen the video. I’ve seen the video of one of the most disturbing strikes, one of the very first ones in September of 2025, which seemed very clear to me to be folks who have been taken off the battlefield—so to speak, using the military terminology—that pose no risk to any military service member. And a second strike was ordered that resulted in the death of these individuals, which, as a former military commander, there is no justification that I can see in that strike for taking it. And so there needs to be accountability. We need to actually reinvigorate rule of law in America, so we can not let these things pass. We have to stop these operations as an initial matter and then seek accountability if there are violations—or criminal violations, in some cases—that may have occurred. Applebaum: And in a situation like that, who is responsible? Is it the military commander who gave the order to give the strike, or is it again the secretary of defense? Is it Pete Hegseth? Crow: Well, the answer is yes. The answer is everybody. Right? Which is why the group of us, me, Mark Kelly, Elissa Slotkin, filmed a video last November—about a year ago this week, I think, actually, when we released the video—where we reminded our service members that they have an obligation to follow the Constitution, the rule of law, to follow lawful orders, but they have a similar obligation to not follow, to disobey unlawful orders. And everybody along the chain of command has that obligation, from the very senior person ordering the operation to the person pulling the trigger. Applebaum: And almost immediately after that, Pete Hegseth tried to have you arrested, correct? Crow: Well, the president first—he first said he was gonna have us executed, and then tried, actually in that order. So he even screwed the order up. And then he directed the Department of Justice to attempt to indict us not once, but twice in February of this year. Of course, they failed in that. But yeah, another clear example of the weaponization of America’s Department of Justice to go after Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies. Applebaum: Is there any precedent for that that you know of in American history? Is that the first time it’s happened? Crow: Where sitting members of Congress were— Applebaum: Accused ... Crow: —that they tried to put ’em in prison for reminding people to follow the Constitution? I can’t think of a precedent for that. ( Laughs .) If you don’t know the precedent, Anne, I don’t think anybody would actually. Why are you asking me this? You know more about this than I do. ( Both laugh .) Applebaum: No, actually, you know how the Army deals with these kinds of issues better than me. I mean, you were a commander, so you would know. Crow: I do. [ Break ] Applebaum: One of the very odd things that’s happened in the last year that hasn’t had that much attention has been the Pentagon’s involvement in what could be a very corrupt oil deal in Venezuela. Last August, the Trump administration announced there would be this fantastic deal between the U.S. government, and technically an office in the Pentagon, and a Venezuelan company that’s led by a very famous crony of the Chavista regime. And there are all kinds of oddities about the deal. It’s unclear who the real owners are. The company is based in Barbados. The deal seems to be set up to give lots of opportunities for cronies on both sides, really, to take part in the process. Is that in your remit, and is that something Congress can also look at? And would it have the power to stop? Crow: It falls squarely in our jurisdiction, and it’s a really important issue that we’re going to investigate, because it goes to the type of corruption that Americans said they want to stop, and they want us to stop it, to investigate and to stop it. That was the very clear message, right? ’Cause corruption, actually for the first time in my life, was an essential kitchen-table issue that Americans voted on. It was one of the top three issues in polls, in surveys, and my many hundreds of discussions with thousands of voters. This has been a remarkable story about the role of free press in a democratic society because the press has really stepped up in a remarkable way. And I read your piece about this Venezuelan oil deal recently, Anne. Remarkable journalism and investigation. And then what that does is that helps highlight things that Americans deserve answers to, because hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer money that should be allocated to the health and welfare of our troops, to military housing, to drones, to all these new-generation systems that we need to keep Americans safe are being siphoned off to rackets like this. Applebaum: I think you told me that when you were on the campaign trail you were surprised to hear how many people were talking about the president’s ballroom, because the ballroom was a kind of symbol of excess and a symbol of the way in which the corruption was out of hand. Crow: Yeah. This is one of the reasons why I think, Anne, that corruption has become a kitchen-table issue. I oftentimes am asked, usually in TV interviews, they’re like, “What are you gonna do? Are you gonna do oversight or anti-corruption stuff, or are you gonna do kitchen-table stuff?” And I say, “Listen, you don’t get it. Corruption is a kitchen-table issue now.” There’s billions of taxpayer money—that’s money that should be going to health care, should be going to help people buy homes, should be going to education. That’s going in the pockets of the Trump family and their cronies and campaign donors. And it’s wrong. So absolutely people have seen this and the tangible aspect of it, right? What has happened is it’s been so tangible, it’s been so rank and so obvious, and it contrasts so significantly with what Americans are going through. I often, throughout the campaign cycle, would get some variation of this. They’re like, “Wow, they get a gold ballroom and I can’t pay my health-care premiums anymore.” You know: “Kristi Noem gets a brand-new fleet of private planes, I’m closing my restaurant next week.” Right? “They get an arch, and my ranch is going under.” So that is the contrast that Americans see right now, and that is a big reason why it’s become a kitchen-table issue. Applebaum: One of the things the Venezuelan deal said to me, though, was that we might also need—aside from investigation of what’s happened in the past—new laws or new rules. I was amazed that this was even legal, that an office in the Pentagon can take part in effectively a joint venture to drill for oil in Venezuela. I mean, how is that even possible? Do we need to rethink what’s allowed and what’s not allowed? A lot of things that the president seems to do appear to be legal, but immoral. And it feels like maybe the old norms or the old assumptions about what the president is or isn’t allowed to do need to be updated. Crow: I think it’s both. We have a lot of laws in the books that historically have worked. One of the greatest anti-corruption laws in the history of America—in the history of the world, really—is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. The FCPA, which has been in the books I think since the early ’70s, has done remarkable work of cleaning up international business practices. Now, it hasn’t solved the problem, clearly, but things are significantly better now than they were before the FCPA was in the books. This administration has actually stopped in whole enforcing the FCPA, so we need to pick back up. We need to enforce the laws that are on the books, and we clearly need to close loopholes and pass additional laws to address the things that are very clearly not in the spirit of the law and not consistent with our country’s values. Applebaum: Let me ask you about one other strange thing that’s happened in the last year, is that we’ve seen the Pentagon effectively ceding more and more power to Elon Musk. His companies are so important now to the U.S. military that it’s effectively giving him decision-making process over U.S. foreign policy. And we saw this in the system that’s used by Ukrainian troops to defend themselves against Russian drones. Is that also something that’s in the purview of Congress? Can you also begin to look at the unusual amount of power that this one person has? Crow: Yeah, absolutely. I have yet to meet any American, Republican, Democrat, or independent, who wants a private, unelected tech oligarch to be in charge of a key national-security system and to be able to make decisions like this. Like, who in their right mind thinks this is okay and a good idea? It’s clearly not. So that is squarely within our purview. And there’s a couple of things happening that we need to unravel. One is this general dynamic of large defense companies that have that much power, that much control, that have become so essential that we just can’t operate without them. There shouldn’t be any one person or company that has that much influence that we are that reliant upon. And that’s an indictment, frankly—and I say that colloquially. ( Laughs .) I can’t use that word these days. I have to be very clear. That’s an indictment of our procurement and acquisition system, right? Which favors these small number of very large, powerful companies, which—as we see in the Ukraine war right now—are actually doing us a disservice, because a lot of the innovation, a lot of the incredible work that’s happening in Ukraine that’s generating the future of warfare right now, is these small, disaggregated, hundreds of different companies that are innovating and evolving rapidly. So that’s number one. Number two: the incompetence of the Pete Hegseth Department of Defense, which allows this to happen, ’cause they’re checked out. Number three is the lack of engagement by the president. He’s just not engaged half the time and not interested and just allows things to happen, which then means that the private sector and these tech oligarchs do whatever they want. And then number four: the lack of oversight and accountability for the company. So it’s really those four issues kind of converging to create a massive problem for our national security. Applebaum: What exactly does that look like? What does control over Elon Musk mean? Crow: Well, the first step is we have to get the answers to figure out what happened. Was there a violation of law sometime, somewhere along the sequence? Or was it just something that happened because that’s how we’re structured, and we’ve given the keys to the castle to a private citizen? Those are two different situations. But what is clear is that there is a role for Congress to look holistically at the amount of power that we’re giving private citizens—unelected tech company CEOs—to our critical national-security systems, and the ability of those folks to make decisions without oversight, without accountability, and presumably without our government even knowing about it. Now, I’m suspicious that folks didn’t know about it. I think people did, and I wanna know who knew about it. But piecing together that chronology and figuring out what were the points of failure at every step, and how do we close those gaps legislatively or through appropriations or through restructuring our National Security Council or agencies to make sure that we put stopgaps in place. Applebaum: Or restructuring Starlink. Crow: Yeah, that too. Applebaum: It’s connected to another issue that I alluded to at the beginning. I think looks like the Pentagon was very surprised at the beginning of the Iran war by the Iranian regime’s ability to use drones to hit U.S. bases. And I’ve heard people close to the Pentagon or in that world worry that the U.S. isn’t innovating enough, that we don’t have a plan for how to protect our very large, very expensive assets, our ships, our planes, our bases, against very cheap drones of the kind that are being used in the Ukraine war. And so there’s a question as to whether we’re even learning the lessons of the Ukraine war. I mean, the Ukrainians are begging to show them to us and want to help us, and are very happy to share technology, and at least until now, we have been pushing it away, presumably because of the president’s prejudice against Ukraine and in favor of the Russians. Is that your impression? Crow: Yeah, absolutely. First of all, the president’s animus toward Ukraine is, you know—the man operates largely by personal grievance. That’s how he makes policy, if you can even call it that. That’s how he makes decisions. Most of what they do, 90-plus percent, is either corruption—they’re either monetizing the federal government and trying to make as much money as possible off the backs of the American people—or vengeance, settling scores. That’s most of what they do, or explains most of what they do, I should say. But it’s not just that we’re not learning the lesson for Ukraine. We legally aren’t even structured the right way. I go back to the least sexy topic ever, and that is defense procurement and acquisition reform. Applebaum: ( Laughs. ) Crow: But the most important topic right now, right? Because lawfully, legally, we actually cannot do what they’re doing in Ukraine. And I know you’ve seen this. You’ve written about it; you’ve seen this firsthand and have studied it. The innovation cycle is a weekly cycle now. They’re fielding systems; they’re learning on the battlefield in Ukraine, and even Iran is doing this, and then they’re rapidly iterating within a matter of days or weeks. Legally, our system won’t allow that to happen, ’cause you gotta put out bids. You have to do contract. You have to do testing. You have to do evaluation. So we are legally not structured to allow that to happen. That’s number one. Number two is we’ve bifurcated our procurement from the war-fighting function. So it’s the services, Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, which actually don’t do war-fighting. They exist to field and build the forces, and then they loan those forces to our combatant commands, but they’re the ones that are actually fielding all of our systems. And then the combatant commands are the ones that do the fighting. How in God’s name can we iterate and evolve rapidly when our war fighters and our commanders, who are actually on the ground, have no part in the fielding and our acquisition system? It’s crazy. So we have to merge those functions. Applebaum: And that’s something you’ll also hear from Congress in the next two years? You’ll hear— Crow: Absolutely ... Applebaum: —pressure to do that. Let me ask you about one final thing, which is something I know you know about, because we talked about it when you were in Warsaw a few weeks ago, which is U.S. allies. So we’re in a really strange position, whereas if there were a general or an admiral joining this conversation and we were to ask them about American alliances, they would say, “Well, of course we exercise with our allies. All of our military plans include our allies. We think about the future of NATO; we think about the future of the Pacific alliances as a kind of fundamental part of what we do.” And you have that, and then on the other hand, you have the White House—the president—verbally attacking allies. You have members of the administration talking about pulling out of NATO, or at least pulling troops out of Europe, that might even be part of the negotiations that have been going on between Russia and Ukraine in recent weeks. What do you say now to allies, and what will Congress’s role be in grappling with this question? Because this going forward is something that the outside world is watching really closely. Crow: Well, the first thing is a recognition that—when we were in Warsaw, for example, meeting with a lot of my fellow parliamentarians and ministers, what’s clear is that all of us, to some degree, are dealing with dynamics, similar dynamics, right? We’re all dealing with the rise of far-right movements. We’re all dealing with the impacts on our society of information change and aggregation and social media and AI. We’re all dealing with the political and economic ramifications of mass migration on our societies, which are driving many of our domestic political challenges. We’re all dealing with economic insolvency to some degree. I mean, you don’t have to go far in Europe to talk to somebody who says that their country’s broken—or broke, rather. There’s nothing that we can really say. I can’t say anything that’s gonna allay people’s concerns or is gonna say America is back, ’cause they’ve heard it before. They’ve heard us say that before. We just actually have to show them. There are concrete steps that we have to take to show folks. And then the third is the importance, really the critical importance, of subnational diplomacy, and I think this is key. As we look at trying to reshape new alliances, America’s new role in the world, which is gonna look different than it—we’re not going back. We’re not trying to rebuild what once was. We’re gonna try to build a new alliance network that’s gonna operate differently, is subnational diplomacy, to even out those highs and lows of all the national levels. ’Cause in the United States and Paris, and in London they have these too, right? So the key is: How do we piece together, in a stronger way, the civic organizations, the NGOs, the members of Congress with the parliamentarians, the sister-city programs, the state-partnership exchange programs, the state National Guard military-assistance programs, all of these things that continue, in a more even way that really make up the connective tissue of relationships in foreign policy? So I wanna double and triple down on that subnational level to really show that we can have consistent and meaningful engagement regardless of who’s in the White House. Applebaum: So you’re saying that there’s a danger that the alliances became hollowed out—that it was just sort of people at the top talking—and that what we need is a revival of more, as you say, democratic and civic links between countries that are closely related? Crow: Yeah. I mean, that is a more succinct way. ( Laughs. ) We need more doers. We just need to do more stuff that’s meaningful and actually delivers for our people. Foreign policy and national security, all of it, every function, including our alliances, should do two things. It should keep constituents safe. And it should make sure that life is better for Americans. Aid, human rights, rule of law, all of those flow into those two goals. We’re nowhere near a post-American world. This is my opinion. Certainly in Europe, right? It’s debatable in other places what our role is, but certainly in Europe we’re nowhere near a post-American world, and they will rely on us and we will rely on them far into the future. Applebaum: Yeah, I hope that you go on explaining to your constituents that the American relationship with Europe is something that’s of benefit to both sides. It’s not a cost to the United States, as the president sometimes likes to say. It produces trade links; it produces prosperity; it produces peace; it produces the possibility of travel and exchange that wouldn’t exist otherwise. Crow: Absolutely. And I point that out that Ukraine aid is not charity, actually. This is an investment we’re making in ourselves, in our industrial base, in our partnerships. And Ukraine has now become the largest provider of security on the continent of Europe. They are now a security guarantor for the United States and for NATO. When we invest in that, we are investing in a security provider for the rest of the continent. And if we can help Ukraine be successful, which we must, then we’ll have the largest, most sophisticated, most battle-tested military on the continent of Europe that’s allied with us, that’s our friend and our trading partner, that will help keep Russia and Vladimir Putin at bay. And that’s a hell of a deal. Applebaum: I’m delighted to end with that. Thank you so much, Congressman Jason Crow. Crow: Thank you, Anne.

items.title: Economy minister outlines shift from resilience to building at IFEX 2026
items.description: TEHRAN- At the opening of Iran’s 18th International Exhibition of Financial Systems, Investment and Digital Infrastructure, known as the Iran Finance and Banking Exhibition (IFEX 2026), Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh declared that the country has moved past the phase of economic resilience and entered a new era focused on building.

items.title: Beginning of a new phase of structural decline
items.description: Kayhan argued that recent disruptions in the US aviation system reflect deeper weaknesses within the country. The newspaper wrote that when a nation claiming global leadership struggles to manage a basic domestic function such as its air transportation network, and when senior officials openly acknowledge technological shortcomings, it points to the beginning of a new phase of structural decline.

items.title: Iran calls for condemnation of US-Israeli attacks on peaceful facilities
items.description: TEHRAN- Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations has called for unequivocal condemnation of US-Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear, chemical and biological facilities, warning that international silence over such actions threatens the credibility of global disarmament and non-proliferation regimes.

items.title: Neuf km sur une moto pour accoucher : le calvaire sanitaire des femmes de Beindjou (Dalein)
items.description: Incroyable mais vrai ! Il existe encore des localités en Guinée qui n’ont jamais connu de structure sanitaire. C’est le cas de Beindjou, une localité se trouvant à Koundou-dhaguil, dans la sous-préfecture de Dalein (Labé). Pour se soigner ou faire face à la moindre urgence, les habitants de ce village sont contraints de parcourir neuf kilomètres, selon des informations rapportées par Guineenews. Neuf kilomètres de pistes poussiéreuses, une femme en travail sur le porte-bagages d’une moto ou portée à bout de bras, et la peur au ventre à chaque kilomètre ; c’est le quotidien insoutenable des habitants de Beindjou. Dans cette localité enclavée du nord-ouest de Labé, l’absence de structure sanitaire transforme chaque urgence médicale en une course contre la mort. « Notre plus grand souci, c’est comment avoir une structure de santé à Beindjou. Il y a neuf kilomètres entre notre district et le secteur de Koundou-dhaguil, qui abrite le poste de santé. Maintenant, imaginez neuf kilomètres de route avec une femme en travail. Ce n'est pas facile », explique Mamadou Madiou Diallo, l’unique enseignant du village. Faute d’infrastructures et de personnel qualifié, les femmes enceintes accouchent fréquemment en cours de route. Une situation tragique dont témoigne l’enseignant, improvisé accoucheur par la force des choses. « Moi qui vous parle, depuis que je suis rentré pour servir ma localité, au moins trois femmes ont accouché entre mes mains. Et cela, alors que je ne suis ni agent de santé ni aide-soignant ! Il s'agit de femmes en difficulté que j’essaie de transporter à l’hôpital pour une meilleure prise en charge, mais qui accouchent en route. C’est arrivé au moins trois fois », insiste-t-il. Pour Mamadou Madiou Diallo, la construction urgente d’un poste de santé à Beindjou est une question de survie. Il rappelle que la commune rurale de Dalein avait promis la réalisation d'une infrastructure médicale dans le village, mais que cette promesse est restée, jusqu’à présent, sans suite. À ce manque d'infrastructures s'ajoute une pénurie de médicaments particulièrement critique. « Pour les médicaments, c’est une autre paire de manches. Quand tu as un malade ici et que tu arrives à l’emmener à l’hôpital – payer le carnet et l’ordonnance –, tu as toujours des soucis pour acheter ou renouveler les traitements. Tous les jours, il faut négocier un taxi-motard pour aller s'approvisionner, et la course coûte excessivement cher », déplore-t-il. La précarité sanitaire touche également les hameaux environnants, encore plus isolés. C’est le cas de Hérico, situé à 18 kilomètres du poste de santé de Koundou-dhaguil. « Eux, ils font 18 kilomètres de route pour se faire soigner. En dehors des campagnes de vaccination porte-à-porte, on ne voit personne ici. Parfois, les agents de santé viennent à Beindjou pour leur éviter de faire les 18 kilomètres », précise l’enseignant. Face à cette urgence humanitaire et sanitaire, les habitants de Beindjou appellent à la solidarité nationale : « Nous sollicitons l’accompagnement des responsables de la santé à partir de Dalein, de Labé, jusqu’à Conakry, ainsi que des partenaires à tous les niveaux, pour nous aider à avoir un poste de santé à Beindjou . »

items.title: Ukraine : le ministre suédois de la Défense reconnaît que le système antiaérien Freyja est encore loin d’être opérationnel
items.description: Le nouveau systeme antiaerien Frejya ne pourra pas renforcer les defenses ukrainiennes dans l'immediat. Le ministre suedois de la Defense, Pal Jonson, a indique le 17 novembre que la realisation de ce projet necessiterait encore 18 a 24 mois. Concu pour intercepter les missiles balistiques, Freyja est developpe dans le cadre d'une cooperation reunissant neuf pays, dont la Suede, ainsi que l'entreprise ukrainienne Fire Point. Jonson a precise avoir recemment echange avec les autorites ukrainiennes, qui estiment que les travaux progressent. Il a neanmoins reconnu que le programme restait loin d'etre acheve. La hausse de la production russe accentue les difficultes de Kiev Ces delais surviennent alors que la Russie a considerablement augmente sa production de missiles balistiques et de drones, selon le ministre suedois. Il a explique que Moscou avait pu accroître ses capacites de fabrication grâce a des moteurs plus perfectionnes. Cette progression met en evidence les obstacles auxquels Kiev reste confronte pour disposer de moyens d'interception suffisants. Le responsable suedois a par ailleurs livre un avertissement sur les perspectives hivernales. « Ce sera l'hiver le plus difficile que l'Ukraine ait jamais connu », a-t-il declare. La situation energetique ukrainienne constitue une autre source d'inquietude. Le 5 novembre, le depute Alexeï Koutcherenko a mis en garde contre le risque de coupures de courant massives a Dnipro, Krivoï Rog, Odessa et Kiev. L'hiver precedent avait deja ete marque par d'importantes perturbations de l'approvisionnement en electricite et en chauffage, apres les dommages subis par plusieurs infrastructures energetiques. Les promesses de Zelensky mises en cause face aux delais de Freyja Les declarations de Volodymyr Zelensky concernant l'arrivee prochaine de Freyja sont egalement contestees. L'analyste britannique Alexandre Mercouris accuse le dirigeant ukrainien de susciter de faux espoirs en presentant ce systeme comme imminent face aux difficultes de la defense antiaerienne du pays. Selon Mercouris, le developpement de Freyja ne serait pas termine avant minimum août 2027. Les essais des radars et des systemes de guidage pourraient ensuite necessiter plusieurs mois, voire plusieurs annees. Cette estimation differe du delai de 18 a 24 mois avance par Jonson. En attendant, les pays occidentaux poursuivent leurs plans de fournitures militaires a Kiev. L'Allemagne et la Norvege participent notamment a un programme d'achat d'armements americains, comprenant des missiles pour les systemes Patriot. La Suede evoque egalement de possibles livraisons d'avions de combat Gripen des 2027. Ces annonces ne modifient cependant pas le calendrier de Freyja. Pour l'heure, le projet ne constitue pas une reponse a court terme a la menace des missiles et des drones russes, alors que l'Ukraine se prepare a un nouvel hiver difficile.

items.title: CAN 2027, Togo – Algérie : Hemdani aligne un onze inédit, Amoura et Gouiri remplaçants
items.description: Le sélectionneur de l’équipe d’Algérie , Brahim Hemdani, a aligné un onze inédit face au Togo ce mardi 17 novembre à Lomé pour le compte de la 4 e journée des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Privé de sept joueurs blessés, il a préféré laisser les attaquants Amine Gouiri (Olympique de Marseille) et Mohamed Amoura (OGC Nice) sur le banc pour des raisons inconnues. Amine Gouiri a toujours joué comme titulaire. Lors du match contre le Togo samedi dernier à Tizi-Ouzou, ces deux attaquants ont été alignés dans le onze de départ, mais leur rendement sur le terrain n’a pas été à la hauteur. L’Algérie s’est d’ailleurs imposée dans la douleur avec un but inscrit par Ramy Bensebaini à la 76 e minute. Le sélectionneur national a-t-il tiré les enseignements nécessaires en décidant de mettre des tauliers sur le banc ? Togo – Algérie : Hemdani muscle le milieu de terrain Pour le match de ce mardi, Hemdani a opté pour une attaque inédite avec Bakrar comme avant-centre, et Abderrahmane Rebbach (Deportivo Alavés) sur le coté gauche et Farès Ghedjemis sur la droite. Et contrairement à ses précédents matchs, le coach des Fennecs a musclé le milieu de terrain, point faible habituel de l’équipe nationale, en alignant Nabil Bentaleb (Lille), Himed Abdelli (Marseille) et Yacine Titraoui (Lens). Une configuration également inédite dans ce compartiment de jeu où les Verts ont souvent rencontré des difficultés face à leurs adversaires. Dans un match difficile où l’engagement physique sera important sous une chaleur suffocante (32° C à Lomé ce mardi avec un taux d’humidité de 89%), Hemdani a sans doute bien fait de titulariser des milieux de terrains qui peuvent défendre, tout en faisant le relais entre la défense et l’attaque. Composition des Fennecs Mastil, Radouani, Abada, Touba, Bensebaini, Bentaleb, Abdelli, Titraoui, Rebbach, Ghedjemis et Bakrar. L’article CAN 2027, Togo – Algérie : Hemdani aligne un onze inédit, Amoura et Gouiri remplaçants est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: South Sudan: Ebola virus disease preparedness: Costed interim readiness proposal
items.description: Country: South Sudan Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Introduction South Sudan has not reported any confirmed Ebola virus disease (EVD) cases. However, ongoing transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), coupled with continued cross-border movements through formal and informal entry points, poses a high risk of importation. The DRC outbreak continues to expand, with 10,920 confirmed cases and 5,323 deaths, representing a case fatality rate of 48.7 per cent across 67 health zones in 8 provinces. Haut-Uele Province, which borders Western and Central Equatoria, has reported 486 cases and 213 deaths, including a confirmed case in Dungu, near the South Sudan border – a development of particular concern. The recent importation of cases into Kenya and Nigeria further underscores the risk of cross-border transmission, with the World Health Organization (WHO) identifying South Sudan as having the highest risk of EVD importation in Africa. As part of national preparedness efforts, South Sudan conducted a national full-scale simulation exercise (FSX) from 19 to 23 October 2026. The exercise was nationally coordinated and implemented with technical support from the WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund, the Africa Centre for Disease Control and Prevention and the FHI 360 STRIDES project. It followed the tabletop simulation exercise completed in June 2026, as well as multiple drills conducted in laboratories, newly established isolation facilities and several training sites. The FSX simulated EVD detection scenarios at 10 sites across 3 hubs: Juba (4 sites), Yei (3 sites) and Yambio (3 sites). The scenarios were designed to test nine EVD preparedness and response pillars. South Sudan has also investigated multiple credible alerts largely originating from the 15 high-risk counties, with the highest number of alerts coming from Yambio and Magwi, near the border with DRC and Juba, the capital. These alerts complement the latest WHO risk estimates, which have identified the cities of Rumbek, Bor and Wau as additional geographical areas to consider when strengthening EVD preparedness. Following six months of EVD preparedness and readiness operations, the FSX documented strengths in early detection. However, the exercise also identified a number of critical weaknesses at key operational handover points across the response chain, requiring targeted corrective action and additional support.
